speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister regarding the reports that are emanating from the NATO meeting in Brussels, where some important decisions seem in the course of being made. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NATO-INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBLE CHANGE IN CANADIAN COMMITMENTS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, no authority has been given to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that would involve any change of commitments on our part. As my hon. friend knows, at the annual meeting of the NATO council the affairs of the coalition generally are discussed, including its defence policies, and proposals made by military headquarters and also by the council.
There has been no authority given and no authority required to make any changes in Canadian policy, nor have any changes been made. Some reports have been made which will have to be considered, and as a result of that consideration there may be changes, but if so the house will have a chance to discuss them. Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words about the increase in the excise tax on tobacco. I fully agree with the sentiments that the hon. member for Edmonton West expressed yesterday. When a government wishes to raise extra revenues through taxation, invariably it ends up by increasing taxes on tobacco and liquor.
Hear, hear.

There is a limit to this sort of taxation, Mr. Chairman. I hope that the minister and the anti-smoking propagandists have not forgotten the lessons to be learned from prohibition in the 1930's. Fortunes were
December 14, 1967

made by those who engaged in bootlegging, smuggling and the illegal manufacture of liquor. The minister will agree with me, I am sure, that nothing is more degrading to a government than to have to engage in the costly business-and I emphasize those words-of stamping out or controlling smuggling, bootlegging, and so on.
The tobacco industry, at least, through the taxes it pays puts half a billion dollars into the pockets of government every year. If the government increases taxes on tobacco and liquor to the point where smuggling, bootlegging and allied activities become attractive, not only will it lose revenue that it otherwise might have gained through taxes but it will need to spend much needed money to suppress those activities.
Another point was put well in an article in the Globe and Mail written by Bruce West. His remarks concisely sum up my feelings about the matter. He said:
I don't like being taxed in the fashion of a naughty little boy being made to pay for his follies.
Then he went on to say:
And by silently accepting each new levy on such things as drinks and smokes, we seem to be admitting that we are bad little characters.
I wish to say to the minister, to the government and to Mr. Bruce West that I am one of those naughty little boys and I will not take the tax increase sitting down. I feel that the limit has been reached in imposing excise taxes on liquor and particularly on cigarettes.
I know it has been some time since the federal government increased the excise tax on tobacco. The last increase took place in 1959. That merely illustrates the point I am trying to make. Away back in 1942 there was a tax increase on tobacco and there were other increases in 1943, 1951, 1952 and 1959. Obviously, since the tax has not been increased since 1959, the government must have realized that the limit in excise tax on tobacco had been approached. The latest increase brings the excise tax to the maximum amount that can be imposed. It is the limit.
As I said previously, the tobacco industry alone brings approximately $500 million to the coffers of the government. At the present time there is dissension in the house about whether medicare ought to be introduced. Some say it should be introduced and others say that because of our present economic position it should not be introduced. I will not go into the merits of the argument but I will
Ways and Means
say that the tobacco industry by itself, through the taxes it pays, could support a large part of the medicare program. In fact, if anyone ever stopped to think about it, the tax that the tobacco industry pays in one year enabled the St. Lawrence seaway to be built.
I acknowledge that excess use of tobacco may be as bad for one as excess use of anything else. A friend of mine died through an excess use of coffee. He drank 40 cups a day approximately. Nevertheless, tobacco has brought a lot of enjoyment and relaxation to many. When one considers what a night editor has to do in editing some of the reports which come out of Ottawa, surely it can be said with truth that if he had no cigarette, pipe or cigar to help him to relax his nerves his life may be very, very short. The same may be said of active businessmen, secretaries and many others who work under tension. Tobacco was a great boon to our boys who were fighting overseas. When they were under heavy fire their nerves were raw and often they preferred to sit down and smoke a cigarette or pipe instead of eating food. I know that chaps who have served overseas will agree with that statement.
I sincerely hope the minister and the department have decided that the present tax represents the limit in taxation that can be imposed on tobacco. These remarks apply equally to another product over which the minister has jurisdiction. Taxes on this product have also been raised recently.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to make a few comments on the question of cigarette smoking. Many of us were very pleased when we heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare announce a few days ago that this subject was to be referred to a committee for consideration. I have been very interested in this question ever since the former minister of national health and welfare told us that a fund of $600,000 would be set up to study the subject of cigarette smoking and its effects. Since that time almost $400,000 has been spent on this project and studies have been undertaken which indicate the hazards caused by cigarette smoking.
December 14, 1967

In spite of this, however, and notwithstanding medical advice and the publicity given to this subject by the news media, statistics show that the sale of cigarettes has been increasing. In view of the fact that such large amounts of revenue are being obtained by the government from tobacco taxes, I feel some action should be taken to provide the safest possible cigarette filter.
In this connection I was interested to receive a letter from the chairman of a senate committee in the United States which is making an investigation into the subject. There is one paragraph in this letter from Senator Warren Magnuson which I should like to put on record.
Last August, the Senate commerce committee held two days of hearings on the progress which is being made toward the development and marketing of a less hazardous cigarette.
I feel that Senator Magnuson's committee has an important task on its hands and I hope it will be found that more research in this direction is necessary. Should this be the case I hope the Minister of Finance will look favourably on any request by the Department of National Health and Welfare or the National Research Council for any assistance desired in finding the safest possible filter for the smokers of Canada in order that they may have a choice available to them instead of smoking cigarettes which we feel are bad for their health.

Mr. Chairman, I am rather glad of this opportunity to make an addendum to the speech I delivered when the budget was introduced. I was, as it were, cut off in my prime and in full flight on that occasion.
I should like to make a passing reference to begin with to the strange discrepancy between the two sides of this budget. I have no doubt whatever that the minister will tell us he combined the two possible courses open to him. One was, of course, to contain expenditure and the other was to increase revenues. Technically he would be quite right. But if we notice the order of magnitude of the two parts we see it is a strange chemical mixture he has produced. His plans, according to his own figures, will bring him in only $270 million extra in a full year. On the other hand, his partner, the Minister of National Revenue-
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

Partner in crime.
Ways and Means

I take it for granted people will realize that the minister is his partner in crime but I will say "his partner" and leave it at that-presented the house with a series of cuts in government expenditures which amount to some $1,200 million.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it is not possible to make cuts of that magnitude without very severe repercussions on the entire economy. Any adding that the minister did in the way of adding to his revenues was a very halfhearted attempt. I am not going to go over again the list of alternatives for revenue which I derived from the repsrt of the Carter commission, but I would like to point out that in this morning's Globe and Mail it is reported that Canadian corporation profits are up by 2.6 per cent over last year, which would at least gently indicate there was another place where the minister could have got some of his revenues.
I think we have to examine the possible reasons for this action because it is too simple to say that the minister is really another Scrooge and just loves to increase taxes.
I would like to ask the hon. member a question in French if he does not mind.
Please do.

Does the hon. member not know that during the forthcoming fiscal year, half of the additional revenue of the federal government will result from the fact that we have compelled corporations to advance their payments to the treasury by two months, and that half of our revenue for the fiscal year, following this mini-budget, already accrues from corporations? In budgetary terms, that revenue represents an additional tax for corporations for the forthcoming fiscal year, that is 1968-69.

I would point out to the Minister without Portfolio that this is a one-shot business. You are merely advancing it and getting the money earlier than usual. Therefore there win be a longer period between the time of that payment and the next payment to accommodate that change. It is really no increase in revenues.

December 14, 1967
Ways and Means
We have to examine the circumstances in which the minister found himself and which to my mind probably induced him to take this rather disastrous course of action. To do that we have to make a brief review of the events which led up to the pegging of the Canadian dollar at 92J cents American.
From 1950 to 1962 the Canadian dollar was on a floating exchange rate and in all those years it oscillated within a very narrow band of 3 cents American, never extending either way beyond that 3 cents. Then in June, 1961, there came a very dramatic change and our dollar rose to over 100 cents American. The next month it went up to 103 cents American and by the end of 1961 and the beginning of 1962 it was running as high as 10 cents over the American dollar, understandably causing very serious repercussions on the Canadian economy. Exporters began to encounter difficulties. Import prices rose with a consequent effect on the whole range of prices. I think we should now look at the next cause.
The development which triggered this explosive rise was a massive inflow of American capital, possibly due to the policies of the Canadian government of the day, and the policies of the Bank of Canada which produced high interest rates in Canada and attracted this inflow. The next stage was reached when the United States government took steps to stem the outflow of capital from that country and brought in the interest equalization act. Immediately the government of Canada, by this time the Liberal government, sent representatives to Washington to beg that Canada be exempted from the operations of that legislation. They succeeded in getting that exemption but had to pay a price for it, and the price was that the Canadian government would maintain its holding of reserves at a certain level, some $2.4 billion or $2.5 billion.
From that moment on, Mr. Chairman, the government of Canada was in a strait-jacket. It was unable to use monetary policy as an instrument to promote economic growth. All its policies had to be tailored to the twin problems of maintaining the tight rate of the Canadian dollar and keeping our reserves below that ceiling. I may say that only a few weeks ago the Bank of Canada had to get into the market to press the Canadian dollar down a bit and in doing so added to our holding of American dollars, showing that these two policies are incompatible. But more important, Mr. Chairman, these two policies

together have tied the hands of the government.
I suggest that if the Minister of Finance hopes to get out of the bonds which he is in now-I am sure he realizes it is a very difficult situation, if not politically very dangerous-he has to take some rather drastic and decisive actions. The first of these, I think, would be to free the exchange rate. It is difficult to forecast with any certitude what would be the immediate result of freeing the Canadian dollar and having it on a floating exchange rate. However, the last occasion is not long ago when the Bank of Canada had to move into the picture to control an upward pressure on the Canadian dollar, and in today's particular circumstances the American dollar is under pressure following devaluation of sterling. So I think it is safe to assume the pressure would be upwards. If that were the case the government would be free to pursue an expansionary policy, to expand the money supply and promote growth and production in Canada.
However, with our minds on what took place in 1961 and 1962 we would also have to take some steps to see that history would not repeat itself. There would have to be some control over inflow and outflow of capital. We could not afford another massive inflow of the type which threw the whole exchange situation out of gear in 1962. There would have to be some controls in that regard. I think it is time the government of Canada looked at the outflow of capital and ceased always parroting the plea that we require massive importation of foreign capital, without paying attention to what is taking place in the economy at the present time. These are two of the things I think the government will have to do.
Then, there is the problem of controlling the type of inflation we have today. As I said the other day, I was interested to hear the minister say he understood it was not a demand type of inflation. This left me very perplexed because the only way in which his budget could make sense would be if it were a means of controlling a demand type of inflation, since it was directed toward cutting down on consumer spending, toward a contraction of the economy of the sort that should take place if there is a rapid development of a classic type of inflation, of too much money chasing too few goods. No one, not even the minister, suggests that the present inflation is of that type. But he is unwilling or perhaps unable to take the only sort of inflation control measures that must
December 14, 1967

be taken in the circumstances of a cost-push type of inflation. He is not prepared to move in the direction of selective price controls on basic commodities whose costs enter into all other costs of the economy.
I know the minister will take refuge in the constitutional position and suggest, technically quite rightly, that this is beyond the powers of the federal government, that only the provincial authorities have jurisdiction over price controls. But I suggest, Mr. Chairman, it would be a very bold provincial government indeed that would be prepared to defy the federal Minister of Finance if he placed before them the necessity for them to exercise their constitutional power to control prices, and if he accompanied that with a well-planned publicity program. In such circumstances I cannot conceive of any provincial government in its right mind persisting in refusal. It would be not only politically disastrous but also economically disastrous, as any such provincial government would be refusing to alleviate the situation of its own citizens.
I want to return for a moment to the question of the control of inflow of capital. For long I have been very doubtful of the statements made time and time again about how dependent we are on an inflow of capital. When I examine the figures I find we have a very small net inflow. I think there was only some $85 million last year as the balance left over following an outflow of some $1,300 million. When we examine some of the ways in which this inflow capital has been used we cannot help but be struck by the extravagant and wasteful ways in which that capital has been invested.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
For instance, as I believe my colleague from Waterloo South mentioned the other day, we have invested in the oil industry some $7 billion to develop an industry which is now incapable of operating at any more than 35 per cent of its capacity because it runs up against market values. As one can imagine, half that investment would have produced all the oil wells we require at the present time. However, that capital flowed in without the government exercising any control over its volume or direction. This minister or his successor and this government or its successor will have to consider very carefully the direction of investment in this country by an investment board such as those which exist in many countries whose function it is to select the areas in which
Ways and Means
massive investments will be permitted and those areas in which they will not be permitted.
One may say that this is a drastic alternative to the minister's budget but I suggest, despite the Prime Minister's denial the other day that we have a crisis, that we actually face a crisis of such proportion that only drastic action of this type will enable us to gain control of our economy and to expand and grow by our own decisions in Canada and not be dependent upon the by-products of decisions made elsewhere. Otherwise I can see the minister and his successor staggering from crisis to crisis while our development and growth are inhibited in a way which will not be tolerable to the 20 million people living in Canada who are conscious of the fact that we have vast stores of natural wealth from which they should be able to build a growing and expanding economy without these continuing crises and restrictive measures. I would think that if the minister and the government or the government which follows are not prepared to take this kind of action, eventually the people of Canada will place their hope in a government which will be prepared to take such action. I shall not be here at the time but I shall watch the situation with interest. My colleague from Winnipeg seems to take exception to that, but I should like to point out that the calendar tells me differently.
However, I beg the Minister of Finance to consider very seriously the necessity for these several measures-a return to a floating exchange rate, the exercise of control over the inflow and outflow of capital, selective price controls to control the cost-push type of inflation, and eventually some measure of control over the direction of investment in this country, so that he or some successor will be able to present to the people of Canada a more hopeful and optimistic budget than the minister has been able to present in any of the many many budgets he has presented during his short term of office. Resolution agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, on this resolution there are a few remarks I should like to make in respect of what I consider has taken place with regard to the price of spirits over the past few years and what I consider to be a quite improper practice on the part of the liquor control boards. I refer to the difference between what must be done by the federal and provincial governments when they wish, in effect, to increase the tax on bottled spirits and bottled beer. Under the provincial liquor administrations it is merely as a result of an administrative order that prices are hiked 25 cents, 15 cents, or whatever it may be. Usually it is said to be on the basis of increased costs. No one, of course, is fooled by that sort of transparent justification for a good number of the increases over the past few years. We know it is merely a desire by the provincial administration to take more and more in the way of taxation from this field. An administrative order by a liquor control board, when it is not fully justified by increased cost or by an increased tax at the federal level, can thus put in force a tax without approval by the legislature.
The federal government, however, in order to increase its revenues from wines and spirits must pass amendments to the Excise Tax Act. A certain practice has developed as a result of what the minister proposes. There have been almost immediate increase in prices by some of the liquor control commissions on the stock they had on their shelves and which had already been cleared from bond. This is something which someone in private business would refer to as unconscionable windfall profits and it is something which we always complain about as a result of any tax action that is taken by the government. There is another aspect of this matter involving the activities of some of the liquor

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the house knows, the first paragraph of this resolution proposes a special 5 per cent surtax on individuals, which is imposed on the amount of an individual's basic tax in excess of $100.
December 14, 1967

All those whose basic tax is less than $100 will be exempt, and the tax will not exceed $600.
For the benefit of hon. members who may not be fully acquainted with these terms, it might be suitable to define what the basic tax is. It is defined in section 33 of the Income Tax Act and is used in the computation of the abatement to make room for provincial taxes. It was also used in the calculation of the tax reduction introduced in 1965. It was used in computing the 20 per cent tax reduction for those with very low incomes introduced in 1966, and it is not disturbed by the present proposal.
Basic tax is income tax as computed on taxable income using the graduated rate schedule. This tax is computed before making the abatement on account of provincial taxes and before deducting the 20 per cent reduction with a maximum of $20 introduced in 1966. It does not include the old age security tax, and it is after deducting the 20 per cent dividend tax credit and before deducting any foreign tax credit. Essentially, it is the graduated rate schedule applied to taxable income, and before the abatements for provincial taxes.

Mr. Chairman, could I ask the minister a question? Could the minister explain to the members of the committee the reasons-I am sure there must be some and perhaps in my stupidity I cannot understand them-for the ceiling of $600 of which the minister speaks. In other words, the maximum increase which any person will have to pay is $600. There may not be many people in that income bracket, but surely they are precisely the people who can most afford to pay. I wonder whether the minister could explain this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the reason for putting on the maximum here was exactly the same reason for putting on the maximum when we applied the process in reverse. When the tax was reduced in 1965, we provided that it would not be reduced by more than $600. So when we put a surtax on-this is not a change in the graduated scale of taxes; it is additional to the amount of tax- it was felt that if the process worked in one direction it should work in the other. It was not our intention in 1965 to benefit the rich by reducing their tax by the whole of the deduction from the basic tax. So when we came to apply the surtax we said we should apply the same principle in reverse and not
Ways and Means
apply this surtax as if it were just an ordinary increase in the graduated rates of tax. That is basically the reason why the government applied the principle in both directions, when we reduced it and when we increased it.
Mr. Chairman, it is a fact, is it not, that practically all the reduction made in 1965 was brought back in the budget of 1966?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is quite true. But when we did reduce the tax we neutralized the effect in 1966. When we went in the other direction we applied the same principle as we had when we made the reduction in the amount of basic tax.

Mr. Chairman, since the minister has given his explanation I shall make my comments on the resolution at this time. I did not participate in the budget debate and I am not going to make a budget debate speech now. I have one or two comments to make in addition to those which my colleagues have made with regard to the necessity of imposing taxes and the type of taxes that have been imposed.
I would like to say something about what I believe to be a little bit of nonsense that has been bandied about with regard to the position taken by the members of the New Democratic party, and why we could not possibly support their subamendment. They have taken the position that the minister has completely abandoned the Carter report. As a matter of fact, some of the members of the New Democratic party called for a wholesale implementation of the recommendations of the Carter report. I do not think too many of them were aware of all the recommendations contained in that report because they could not possibly endorse some of them before their so-called supporters. If they did, they would have their hides taken off by their supporters.
* (4:20 p.m.)
You know that?

I have certainly had
representations from the same type of voter who feels that he does not want things like unemployment benefits and other items deemed to be income in accordance with the Carter report; he wants them carefully kept out.
Not all of the representations requested by the minister in connection with the Carter

December 14, 1967
Ways and Means
report have been made. Not all of the provinces have replied. There has been no white paper published, so the house has not had an opportunity to discuss a government white paper on the Carter proposals. Yet we are told that in this particular budget we should have implemented holus-bolus the recommendations in the Carter report.
No one said that.

That statement appeared
time and time again in the speeches of the members of the New Democratic party, and that is certainly their attitude.
Whether or not the minister has abandoned the Carter report is for him to say; I am not going to speak about what he is going to do. However, I will say that having attended the deliberations of the Canadian Tax Foundation, at which were tax lawyers, tax accountants and economists, many of whom support the N.D.P., I think the report merits far more study than it has been given up to now. Anyone who dares suggest that the report should have been implemented, in whole or in part, in this budget is being completely naive. As a matter of fact, this to me is a dangerous attitude to adopt.
I have been trying, Mr. Chairman, to get the minister to refer the Carter report to a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons before the government commits itself to a white paper. I have gone through the deliberations of the tax foundation earlier in November and I am more than ever convinced that I am right in this suggestion. There is a wide divergence of opinion at the academic and professional tax lawyer and tax accountant level. Some very prominent tax accountants and tax lawyers advocate, for example, a capital gains tax. Others are quite in favour of the principle of integration. Others are in favour of the removal of the depletion provisions for the extractive industries, and just as strong views are held the other way.
I would put it to the minister and to the members of this committee that there is no crushing need to implement the provisions of the Carter report. The inequalities in our taxation system have been there for a long period of years. It took a lot of time to determine their exact nature and for the royal commission to make up its mind on the kind of system it was going to recommend. We know the commission based itself on a particular system of taxation advocated by some economists from Chicago, and these

questions have been kicking around for some time.
I think it is certainly open to question whether the commission has fastened upon a tax system that was primarily designed for the United States economy, a capital accumulating economy, and has decided to impose it upon the Canadian economy which is far from capital accumulating but is actually a capital borrowing economy.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I again put it to the minister as forcefully as I can that some members of this house should be appointed to a joint committee with members of the other place. The other place is eminently suited for the long and deliberative study that is required for the consideration of the Carter report and the submissions which have been made to the government. Then this house will be able to make up its mind and in the end we will have a much better result. The government is going to take a certain position for political reasons, and the white paper will commit the government to certain courses of action.
There is no such thing, Mr. Chairman, as being partially in favour of a capital gains tax. I could use another simile and say there is no such thing as being a little pregnant. One is entirely sold with this idea or not. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will reconsider the position and that, in light of certain events which are now taking place and which will take place in the future, the house will be given the opportunity to appoint members of all parties to a joint committee to study the Carter report, instead of the government publishing a white paper first. That is all I have to say with regard to this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I was going to rise in any case to repeat the very strong objections of the members of this party to the measures contained in this resolution, but perhaps I may take a minute or two to answer the strictures directed against the members of this party in connection with the Carter report.
My hon. friend from Edmonton West is wrong in suggesting that any one of us asked the minister to implement the Carter report now holus-bolus. What we said-and I am not going to retract what we said for one moment-was that we were in favour of the principles of the Carter report. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I do not qualify that statement by reference to any particular recommendation as far as I know and
December 14, 1987

understand it, and I hope I know and understand most, if not all, of the recommendations.
I was fully aware when I spoke, as were my colleagues when they spoke, that the minister had not yet completed his studies of the Carter report. I cannot put my hand on Hansard for November 30 so I am going to speak from memory, and no doubt the minister will correct me if I misrepresent him. But what the minister said on that day was this. As I recall, he cited four objections that have been raised to the Carter report and intimated-he did not explicitly state-that he agreed with them. Those four objections were made by what I call the vested interests whom the Carter report was trying to get into the taxation net.
The minister then went on to say, according to my recollection of his remarks, that as far as the government were concerned they were not going to implement the Carter report but would merely amend and revise our present taxation system in what they thought were appropriate ways. In other words, what the minister said was that as far as the basic principle of the Carter report was concerned, which is that all purchasing power from whatever source, whether coming from what we now call income, or transfer payments, or benefits, or from capital gain, that came into the hands of a Canadian citizen, either individual or corporate, subject to the integration of taxes, was to be regarded as taxable.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
That is the principle we accept, Mr. Chairman, and it is the principle that the minister rejected, as I understand the situation. We were, of course, not naive enough to think that the minister should bring in an entire restructuring of the tax system immediately. What we did say to him, and what I say to him without any qualification again today, is that if he was desperately in need of revenue before next spring then he ought to have imposed other taxes. He ought to have immediately removed the concessions to the extractive industries. I shall have something to say in a moment about the absurd position which the minister took. In fact, it is suggested that quite possibly he would have made more out of removing the concessions I mentioned than he could out of increases in the personal income tax. This is what we said, and I do not withdraw from that position for one moment. This is where the money is, and this is where he should have
Ways and Means
gone. I oppose this resolution, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of my colleagues as well as myself. Others may well take the opportunity to tell you this themselves.
I believe that this increase in income taxes is unfair, is unnecessary and in its economic consequences is bad. I do not know why one needs any more reasons to oppose it. It falls on the working people of this country. This attempt to equate the exemption of the first $100 of basic tax with the ceiling of $600 at the other end seems to me a kind of cynical illogic that we should not be willing to accept. In fact, it is a kind of sophistry which is intended to throw sand in people's eyes. The fact is that the exemption of the bottom $100 will mean some people will be exempted from paying an additional $5, that is, 5 per cent on the basic tax of $100. The limit of $600 for any person having an income of about $30,000 or more, as I have calculated, will mean anywhere from $100 to $400 or more. So far as I am concerned, you do not do justice by offsetting $400 or $500 at the top, for the person who can well afford the money, against $5 at the bottom.
This is typical of the justice that I have witnessed in this house, and when I was not in this house, which is often meted out to our people-the equality of one horse to one rabbit, and that is not equality. You do not achieve equity by removing $5 at the bottom, which the rich guy also gets because his first $100 is not taxed either under this proposal, when in addition to that he gets an exemption on anything over $600 which he would have had to pay.
The minister tells us in a soft voice that the reason for this is that in 1965 when there was a reduction of 10 per cent, if I remember correctly, there was a limit of $600 at that level so now he feels morally obliged to have the $600 ceiling when he increases the tax. What nonsense this is. What utter, unmitigated rubbish it is. Of course the other limit was justified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why?

Because the people who pay more taxes at that level can afford to continue to pay more taxes. In any tax system in any society the important thing so far as the individual is concerned is what he has left, not what he pays. If I may bring in a personal note, I recall when I was national secretary of the C.C.F. and getting the amount the C.C.F. could afford to pay; I paid very little tax and I was left with little.

December 14, 1967
When I
much more in taxes but I was still better off. As I say, the important thing is not the amount a person pays but the amount he has left. It was right to establish a $600 limit at the time taxes were reduced because the person at the top could afford to pay more. It is inequitable, it is unjust, it is unfair, it is anti-social so far as I am concerned, to establish a $600 limit when you increase taxes. The person making $50,000 or $60,000 a year-there are not many, but there are some-can afford to pay $1,000 or $1,200 in additional taxes much more easily than the ordinary worker can afford to pay even $1 per week more in taxes.
The increased taxes to which I have referred would not affect the normal living of the wealthy person, whereas an additional $50 for the ordinary working man means cutting down on the necessities of life for his family. When you add to that the increased cost of cigarettes and beer, which are the ordinary working man's luxuries, then you hit him very hard indeed. This is why we oppose this measure. This is why I do not accept this sophistry in respect of the $600 limit. I cannot think of any other reason for this move than that the minister wanted to be kind to the people whom he hopes will buy his bonds. These are the people who have the money with which to buy his bonds. We cannot, under any circumstances, support such a proposition.
The budget is also unnecessary, Mr. Chairman. I do not, for the life of me, see why the minister had to bring down this budget on November 30. Do you know how much the minister will raise in the remaining part of this fiscal year? He will get about $25 million out of the increase in income tax and a total, if I remember correctly, of some $40 million or $45 million including the other taxes on tobacco, beer and spirits. If the minister suggests to this committee that an additional $25 million for the remainder of this fiscal year even begins to touch his problem, he would be less intelligent than I sincerely believe him to be. He will make no such statement. Mr. Chairman, may I comment on the statements which have been made by the hon. members for Edmonton West and York South. The hon. member for Edmonton West repeated his suggestion that the Carter commission recommendations should be referred to a committee of the house for study. I gave serious consideration to this possibility and in a way I am inclined to agree with the hon. member. It will be very difficult to bring down proposals that will satisfy public opinion in this country. Tax reform is one of the most difficult and delicate matters that any government must deal with. Perhaps it would have been easier to remove that responsibility from our shoulders and place it on the shoulders of a committee. Nevertheless, I believe that the government has a responsibility that is very special with regard to the raising of revenues, and I did not think it was in accordance with the traditions of our system of government for the government to say to a committee of the house: Please tell us how to reform the tax system. It is perfectly all right to ask a committee to make suggestions. My hon. friend's government asked a committee to advise the government on suitable methods of tax reform. But I believe that any proposals which are brought before the house must be brought by the government itself.
I also felt that if we were to refer the Carter commission recommendations to a committee the government would only get another advisory report. We had already received a very thorough, indeed, a monumental study on tax reform and we had asked the public to comment on the report. I felt that the time had come for the government itself to bring before parliament a scheme of tax reform.
I recognize, as the hon. gentleman said, that once we have made our recommendations we are to some extent committed to them in the sense that once I have brought down a budget I am committed to it, since the government stands or falls-
Unless you change your mind.

Unless we change our minds, that is right.

Mr. Chairman, the discussion was warming up and becoming so interesting that I would willingly have allowed it to go on, but I should like the time to explain why I intend to vote for the minister's bill and say why.
I say immediately that it is not because I find it perfect, and I have heard a good many suggestions that I would willingly support, but I also have heard the minister call for suggestions and criticisms, because he realized better than anyone else in the house that this is a most complicated situation which it is not easy to settle.
Here, Mr. Chairman, is an outline of the reasons why I propose to support the government.
First, I believe it is important inasmuch as I am concerned at least, to state that I have no partisan interest in doing my utmost to bring the government down. On the contrary, I believe it is important to do everything I can to ensure a certain stability to the government. I find the present system of exposing the government to non-confidence motions, one after the other, to have the sword of Damocles constantly hovering above your head, is an inconsistent way of doing things in our advanced world. In view of the complicated problems that have to be settled, the governments should be assured of some stability, four or five years in office, so that they may have the time to arrive at policies, the good or bad results of which can then be observed.
If the government errs, we will have an election campaign during which we will have the opportunity of making them-and the electors-understand the error of their ways, but it seems to me that the tendency to bring down the government every five or six months is futile, childish and out-of-date in the complicated world in which we live.
There is another reason, Mr. Chairman. It is that in the field of finance and taxation, we realize today that the problem is worldwide and complicated, to the point where even an expert like the minister who has

spent a lifetime in the field and who is surrounded by experts in the matter, who has met experts in taxation and in international finance of every country of the world, himself recognizes, as he has this afternoon, that he has trouble in finding equitable solutions.

We are opposed to the particular proposals because they are completely unfair. If ever there was a class budget, this is it. This budget is designed to increase the burden of the ordinary taxpayer and let those people who have large incomes get away almost scot free. A 5 per cent surtax will mean that the bulk of the money raised will be from income tax paid by those in the lower or middle income brackets. The provision to which the minister referred relating to a maximum of $600 which can be paid by anyone exempts those people who can most afford to pay increased tax from paying their share. I think the minister said there were
32.000	people in the income bracket that will be required to pay increased taxes to the extent of $600. It may well be that not much money will come in as a result of the 5 per cent surtax collected from these very wealthy people, but the fact is that this sets a very poor example because the ordinary citizen will have to pay the full increased tax while
32.000	wealthy people will have a limit in respect of what they must pay.
The minister said again that he had not rejected the recommendations and basic principles in the Carter commission report. He put on the record again this afternoon what he said earlier. No matter how thin the minister slices the boloney, it is still boloney. The facts are very clear. The minister proposes by this mini-budget to increase the personal income tax and ignore entirely the recommendations of the Carter commission. These recommendations may be accepted at some later date but in light of the situation it is pretty obvious to most of us that the majority of the Carter commission recommendations will be forgotten.
The minister has tried to scare us off by telling us and the Canadian people that we surely do not want unemployment insurance classified as income and therefore taxed. He asks us whether we want veterans benefits classified as income and therefore taxed. He says that surely we do not want these things

but he did not say today, though I am sure he will on another occasion, that we do not want members of co-operatives to pay tax on their co-operative patronage dividends.
What the minister is doing in defence of the mining industry, the oil industry and other business interests is chipping away from the basic concept the Carter commission enunciated in respect of its support of the interests of low income bracket group. I do not think it makes any difference whether the minister talks about a tax rate of 50 per cent, 45 per cent or 55 per cent. What the Carter commission stated was that essentially the low and middle income groups in this country were paying an unfair share of the taxes collected while the higher income group is getting away with a limited tax.
What has the minister said about this situation? Has he made one single proposal to plug the loopholes documented so very well by the Carter commission? He has not, and I do not think he will because he represents a constituency made up of people who are in the high income bracket.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, veterans.

The minister has not said a word about the large number of people in the upper income bracket who do not pay a penny income tax in terms of expense accounts. He does not say anything about the large number of people who are in the position to deduct a very substantial part of their car expenses on the basis of being a business expense whereas the ordinary construction worker who may have to travel 25 miles each way between his home and his job cannot do this because this cost of transportation is not considered a business expense. The minister has not said a word about the number of people who deduct conference expenses. I have in mind a group of doctors who hold annual meetings in different cities and different countries. Recently this conference was held on a ship travelling the Caribbean. The cost of this was a legitimate business expense and deductible for income tax purposes. We have not heard a word about this sort of thing being inherently wrong.
The minister has not said a word about the basic recommendations of the Carter commission. The commission suggested that oil, mining and insurance companies are not paying a fair share of the taxes. The minister tries to create the impression that we are all animals of a strange kind because we think these people should be paying their share of
December 14, 1967

taxes. In the event that the minister has been too busy to read the Toronto newspapers, let me draw his attention to a couple of editorials which appeared this month in the Toronto Star. This newspaper at election time will promote the interests of the Liberal party and urge Canadians to elect Liberal candidates in all parts of Canada. Let us look at what the Toronto Star said about the minister's tax proposals and how he ignored the basic recommendations of the Carter commission. The editorial suggests that he has buried these recommendations but I think he has killed them. This editorial, which appeared in the Toronto Star of December 7, 1967 under the heading "Have The Insurance Firms Won", includes the following paragraph:
It noted that Canadian insurance companies, with 30 per cent of their business placed abroad, paid $ 13.800,000 in income taxes to foreign governments. It pointed out in contrast that foreign insurance companies in this country paid no income tax to Canada on life insurance policies written in this country.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The editorial went on to say:
The 1964 revenues of Canadian insurance companies exceed their expenditure by $90 million. But they paid tax on less than $5 million of that amount.
The report acknowledged that insurance premiums might have to be raised, or policy dividends reduced, if insurance companies were required to pay their fair share of income tax.
But the commission clearly believed that this was wholly acceptable since it would mean a substantial increase in federal revenues and a consequent easing of the tax load on the ordinary taxpayer.
These were reasonable and just proposals, long overdue. Are they now to be discarded by Mr. Sharp because of pressure from the insurance companies?
I think it is obvious that they have been discarded by the Minister of Finance. In an editorial which appeared a few days later on December 11, entitled "Mines Should Pay Fair Tax Share", the Montreal Star said:
How can finance minister Mitchell Sharp justify his decision to dig new tax revenue out of the ordinary wage earner while continuing to provide special tax privileges to big business-notably the mining industry?
The Carter Royal Commission on Taxation found that mining, along with the insurance and petroleum industries, was a potentially rich source of tax revenue that had long been enjoying unnecessary exemptions.
It is estimated in this editorial that the amount the mining industry would have paid, calculated on 1964 figures, if they had paid the ordinary taxes which all businesses 27053-3431
ways and Means
except mining, oil and insurance pay, was somewhere between $133 million and $250 million annually. It is for this reason that we say-and we are not alone in saying it, as I have pointed out-that the minister, despite all his protestations, has killed the basic recommendations contained in the report of the Carter commission.
The minister has ignored another basic recommendation of the Carter commission, namely, that Canada should do what nearly every other modern industrial country has done and implement a capital gains tax. If such a tax were imposed it would bring into the coffers of the Canadian government tens, if not hundreds, of millions of dollars. To the extent that this is not done, and for each year in which it is not done, the ordinary taxpayer is paying substantially more income tax than he should be paying. Yet the minister gets up again and again and says he is not ditching the Carter commission recommendations. I will believe that the minister is not ditching them when he brings in proposals to tax the mining, insurance and oil industries. I do not think I will be in this house long enough-and I expect to be here for some time-to see the Minister of Finance do that, because he believes, as apparently his government does, that those industries which have shall continue to have and those which have not shall pay taxes. That is precisely what the minister has done in implementing the 5 per cent surtax on income and the extra tax on beer and tobacco.
If we take the minister's budget speech together with the speech of the Minister of National Revenue in which he announced very substantial cut-backs in government expenditures for next year, we can come to no other conclusion than that there will be substantially more unemployment next year than there is this year. We reject such a policy. We reject it nationally and even more emphatically in terms of regional welfare and development.
It may not be a very serious matter to booming areas such as Toronto and Vancouver if the government cuts back on its expenditures. But I say to the minister and to some of the members of the official opposition who have been saying, if I understand them correctly, that the fault of the government is that it has not cut expenditures enough, that to impose the kind of cut-backs which the government proposes in the slow growth areas of this country is a disaster.

December 14, 1987
Ways and Means
While contractors may be building new factories, shopping centres, houses and apartment buildings at a record rate in central Canada in the Toronto and Hamilton areas, if you take away government expenditures in the Atlantic provinces there will be nothing left. I was there about a month ago at the invitation of railway workers. At that time I visited Sydney. I cannot remember when I spent a more depressing day, because I heard about lay-offs in the coal mines, in the steel mill, lay-offs of railway workers and longshoremen at North Sydney.
The proposals of the government to cut back expenditures mean that the unemployment situation in our slow growth areas will be of catastrophic proportions in the coming year. We do not agree that government expenditures need to be cut back at all. Certainly I will never agree that government expenditures should be cut back by the meat-axe method which the Minister of National Revenue announced the other day, while there is not the slightest sign of intention by the government to do anything to in any way restrict expenditures in the private sector of our economy.
I remember that when the Minister of Finance brought down his budget last year, I think it was in February, he announced not the cut-backs which we have had announced now but some kind of pause. I remember that the minister announced one specific project that would not be proceeded with. This was a building here in Ottawa which the government had previously agreed was necessary, namely, a building for the National Research Council.
The day after the minister made his speech announcing that pause, the day it was reported in the Ottawa newspapers that the government would not go ahead with this building, in the Ottawa Jouvnal, and I presume in the Citizen too, there was a two-page spread about the new hotel-office building complex within a few blocks of the parliament buildings which Campeau Construction Company Limited was going ahead with. I have no objection to another hotel being built in Ottawa. Perhaps it is needed. But as far as I am concerned we needed the building for the National Research Council a great deal more that we did the Skyline hotel. If we must have restraints, let us have them in respect of those things which are not necessary. We would be somewhat more sympathetic to the minister's ideas on restraints if 
we thought they would be applied to things we can do without.
At the housing conference which took place the other day, which I think ought not to have been proceeded with if the federal government could not increase the amount of money it was prepared to devote to housing, the premier of Ontario, Mr. Robarts, and the premier of Quebec, Mr. Johnson, made what I thought was a very worth-while proposal.
It was not a proposal that would cost the federal government money. It was in relation to houses whose cost, exclusive of land, did not exceed $15,000.
a (5:40 p.m.)
The Assisiant Deputy Chairman: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but while the Chair has allowed quite a bit of straying from the resolution now under study I think the hon. member is going a little farther than his predecessors. I therefore ask him to come back to the resolution under study.

Mr. Chairman, I think I am precisely on the paragraph we are studying. I am trying to illustrate why I intend to vote against this 5 per cent surtax on income tax. First of all I am suggesting that we do not need this increase in taxes and, second, that if restraint is needed it should be in more sensible fields. One area in which we do not need restraint is that of housing.
The suggestion of the premiers of Ontario and Quebec was that if the federal government would rebate the sales tax on building materials used to construct relatively modest homes, the governments of Ontario and Quebec would in turn be prepared to rebate from their provincial coffers the provincial sales tax on building materials. They calculated that the federal and provincial rebates would amount to between $1,200 and $1,500. In other words, the two rebates would be sufficient to raise the down payment on a house.
I thought this was a very sensible and modest proposal that the federal government would jump at, but it did not do so. It is opposed to this kind of planning, to this kind of common sense. The federal government wants to charge everybody tax.
I suggest that people who build shopping centres, service stations and luxury office buildings can well afford to pay this tax. Why not? They merely pass the increased cost on to their customers. However, the ordinary citizen who wants to buy a house simply cannot afford this extra tax, so less and less people are buying houses.
December 14, 1967

This government simply refuses to interfere in the slightest way with the private sector. When there is need for restraint the restraint is focused upon the public sector. The federal government is setting an example which I am sure it hopes the provinces and municipalities are going to follow. If they do, then it means there will be a cutback in the building of schools. This is precisely the area in which the economic council, among others, has said we need to increase our efforts. It has already been announced that there is going to be a cutback in the building of new health facilities. As a matter of fact, the Minister of National Revenue has announced that the money from the health resources fund which goes toward assisting the provinces and universities in the building of medical colleges will have to be stretched out.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I
am sorry to interrupt the hon. member again but this resolution is to amend the Income Tax Act.

But is that not precisely the point, Mr. Chairman? The minister is increasing income tax because he needs more money. If the government needs more money I am suggesting it should look at the expenditure that is being made. Because I do not like the proposals of the minister for the spending of money I am outlining as briefly and as closely to the resolution as I can the reasons I intend to vote against this measure.
I am not going to go into the arguments presented by the leader of my party, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, who referred to items of useless military expenditure such as the Bonaventure, the supporting destroyers and obsolete aircraft. We are pouring not small amounts, Mr. Chairman, but hundreds of millions of dollars into this sort of equipment.
I am suggesting to the Minister of Finance that he should manage the economic life and social needs of the country in such a way that the ordinary citizens are given some equity. Instead of doing this he is indicating clearly that he believes in the maxim that those that have shall continue to have. Until he changes his views he will not get support from the members of this house.

Mr. Chairman, I want to deal very briefly and basically with a comment made by the Minister of Finance which rather disturbed me. However, I must say that I do not rise as an authority on fiscal
Ways and Means
and budgetary affairs; I leave those matters to persons who have given them much more study than I and who have been more successful in forecasting financial affairs than I have in my lifetime.
I rise first of all, Mr. Chairman, because I thought the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West was a good one. He suggested that the Carter report go before a committee of this house or, if I understood him correctly, before a committee of the Senate.
Both.

Yes, or both. I think that is a good suggestion. I have argued for a long time that we should make much greater use of committees in the Senate when dealing with particular problems. These committees have done some good work in the past in such matters as manpower, land use, and so on, and they might well study other current questions instead of our spending large sums of money on royal commissions.
I understand why there is some hesitation on the part of the government in implementing the Carter report, because there have been widespread objections. The farmers organizations of Canada have objected on certain grounds to certain proposals in the Carter report. The beef producers have objected on certain grounds to other proposals. So have the fruit growers and the cooperatives. The national credit union has made strong protests against the effect of the application of certain proposals in the Carter report. Some unions have also objected to the implementation of certain sections in the Carter report, as have some large companies.
These larger companies have mostly been concerned with making representations to protect their write-offs and that sort of thing. However, I cannot understand why they did not have enough common sense and understanding of public relations to bring the plight of other people to the attention of the government when they were making their own representations.
The Royal Canadian Legion has been concerned about some of the proposals in the Carter commission report. As a matter of fact the Legion has written a letter to the Prime Minister explaining the attitude of their members. So have the army and navy veterans and other veterans organizations across the country. I have had a lot of correspondence on this matter and can fully appreciate

December 14, 1967
Ways and Means
their attitude to proposals in the Carter commission report that would tax veterans disability pensions. It was largely a comment of the Minister of Finance that stirred me for a moment or two to say a few words.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This has been a matter of great interest to me since I was president of a Great War Veterans Association branch in 1919. I was one of those who helped prepare the resolution which was presented to the government urging exemption from taxation of disability pensions. In that connection I have some extracts from Hansard of the day. I recall the change in the attitude of the government at that time. This matter was brought to the attention of the house on June 13, 1919 by Sir Herbert Ames and Mr. Lemieux. As a result of their representations Sir Thomas White, who was minister of finance at that time, had this to say:
I am disposed to regard very favourably the suggestion put forward by the two bon. members. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) had drawn the matter to my attention and it strongly appeals to me. It is not necessary to make any amendment to the resolution, because it is open to us, when the bill is in the committee stage, to extend the exemptions by cutting down and not adding to the burdens of taxation. I will have a note made of the suggestions and get an appropriate amendment to the bill when it is in the committee stage.
Later, on June 24, the same question came before the house and the minister of finance, Sir Thomas White, had this to say:
I am glad to have the matter drawn to the attention of the Commissioner of Taxation.
I now wish to move an amendment by inserting the following clause immediately before clause 4:
"4. Section five of the said Act is amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:-
(i) Income derived from any pension granted to any member of His Majesty's military, naval or air forces for any disability suffered by the pensioner while serving in any of His Majesty's forces during the war that began in August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen, and the income derived from any pension granted to any dependent relative of any person who was killed or suffered any disability while serving in the said forces in the said war."
I think that meets the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) and concurred in by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux).
This was agreed to unanimously by the house at that time. When this amendment was passed the government received letters of thanks from the various veterans organizations, including the Great War Veterans Association, for taking this humanitarian approach. I was closely associated during

that period in the organization of the Great War Veterans Association. I remember it quite vividly. This principle has been accepted by parliament since 1919 and there has never been any suggestion of varying it until the Carter commission report was made public. This caused concern amongst a number of veterans organizations across Canada including the Royal Canadian Legion, and that is why the president of that organization wrote the Prime Minister a personal letter on this question.
This principle was endorsed by all parties at that time and has been endorsed by all parties until this date. They realize it is a humanitarian principle. Not only has it been endorsed in Canada but it is followed by almost all democratic countries. In order to illustrate this point I want to quote from the World Veteran for July-September, 1967, which contains a report of the proceedings of the international conference on legislation concerning veterans and war victims. When the standing committee on veterans affairs was in Europe in 1966, the members had an opportunity to meet with the executive of this organization and to attend one of their meetings. I was surprised because this organization, which represents veterans from about 50 countries in the world, is doing excellent work in connection with the promotion of world peace. It may interest some people to know that Colonel So-and-so, Major So-and-so and Brigadier So-and-so were sponsoring resolutions directed toward the promotion of peace in the world. Why did they do so? Those who have served in war or have suffered in war are usually the ones who are most concerned about maintaining peace in the future.
As I have said, most countries in the world exempt disability pensions from taxation. This matter came up for discussion again at this conference and the following resolution was passed:
Considering that war victims pensions are compensation for injuries occurred or for the loss of family members;
Noting that financial means for them are provided by the whole population of a country concerned through taxation;
Recommends governments concerned to decide that the compensation provided by war victims legislation be exempted from tax.
This is the accepted practice. I think we all realize that throughout the years it has been the practice of this government to exempt disability pensioners and their dependents from income tax on their pensions. It has
December 14, 1987

been the policy of the government in connection with workmen's compensation payments. It has been the policy of the government not to tax civilian disability payments or allowances. I urge on the members of this house, therefore, that they continue to support this humanitarian principle that has been in effect in our country since 1919. I can tell you that as a veteran and a socialist you will not get me to support any other policy.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance made a number of assertions with which I want to deal for a few minutes. I may say, first of all, that the minister made what I suggest was a basic distortion of the meaning and intent of the Carter report by trying to indicate that because there may be some details in it about which some may have questions, this means the Carter report as a whole is affected. It may well be that the disability pensions of veterans which are paid as a result of the gratitude of a country for service in war ought not to be included for income tax purposes. I have a strong feeling of agreement with this principle. There are one or two other benefits of a similar kind that ought not to be included in income. It may well be, therefore, that the Carter commission in seeking to put up a completely logical device did as a good many logicians have done many times in history, failed to recognize some of the exceptions which make logic stronger rather than weaker.
But when the minister suggests that these possible exceptions from the general framework of the Carter report justify him in ditching the report as a whole, he is treating the members of this house and the people of Canada as if they were children.

Read his words.

On clause 1-Incorporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, this bill might be said to be the twin of another bill that the house considered the other day, though the bills are not related. When this matter was being discussed in the house previously the hon. member for Skeena and other hon. members of this party objected to the wording of the bill. The company seeking incorporation has sought powers to carry on activities which are wholly beyond its means. As I understand it, the company specifically wishes to build a pipe line between Lloyd-minster and a storage point in Saskatchewan. In addition to seeking power to build such a pipe line the company, through clause 6 of the bill, seeks the power to carry on a great

December 14, 1967
Private Bills
many other activities. A great many of the powers that are being sought are not needed and I hope that the company will see fit to withdraw its request for some of these powers if it wishes this bill to receive favourable consideration by this house.
I am sure that the sponsor of the bill will agree that a radar chain is very expensive to build and that the $4 million capitalization of this company will not cover the cost of such a chain. I am sure that the company's money will not be enough to cover the construction of one microwave tower. Certainly the company will not build an airport and it will not buy aircraft for that airport. It cannot provide its aircraft with an adequate communications system. In short, Mr. Chairman, by being asked to accede to these powers which are listed in clause 6 members of parliament are being made to look like damn fools. The company obviously will not undertake everything that it seeks power to undertake under clause 6.
I have asked officials of the Senate if they can correct what is becoming an increasing problem. I am informed that representatives of companies such as this one which wish to become incorporated look at a copy of a bill that has recently been passed and adopt many of the provisions which have been included in such former bills. That, I suggest, has happened in this instance.
It is possible that some day this company will gather, process, refine, treat, transmit, transport, store and deliver gases, liquids and solids or any of them, but I very much doubt that in the foreseeable future the company will wish to bring about the expansion of a four inch pipe line. That is a very small pipe line. Its diameter is about one third of that of the pipe line which is now being laid on Kent street in Ottawa. The municipal authorities are forever laying new pipe lines on Kent street. From personal observation I would say that the pipe line on Kent street is an eight inch or a ten inch pipe line. Certainly such a pipe line would carry three or four times the gas that the pipe line which this company is to build will carry.
One thing is clear, Mr. Chairman. If this company wants to build a four inch pipe line I suggest that it must ask parliament for permission to do so. If they do not ask for that permission they will meet with little success in their application. They must say what they want to do.
Having listened to the hon. member for Provencher who is sponsoring this bill I realize that the idea of transferring gas to dry

wells from which it can be drawn during peak consumption periods is a worthy one. The idea makes economic sense and seems to be economically sound. I think the company would be well advised to go ahead with some of the projects it proposes but not with all these projects. In my opinion the company is not capable of developing some of these other projects for which they are seeking approval. I refer among other things to the clause which speaks about facilities for communication, the installation of teletype, microwave or television communication systems, and so on. Possession of these rights would mean that the licences could probably be sold as a step toward setting up a third broadcasting system in Canada. I do not suppose this will happen and I am sure the sponsor of the bill will tell us that the company does not have this in mind. I agree that when a licence is granted to a pipe line company it is advisable for the company to ask for assent to arrangements which would provide for certain types of communication to be carried on in connection with its operations but these, I suggest, would fall outside the Broadcasting Act or the Radio Act.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
No one can foresee some of the needs which may develop in connection with pipe lines. It may be possible for pipe lines to be fitted with closed circuit television which will allow for the observation of the progress of packaged capsules within a line. But I am sure that no company would establish a closed circuit television operation in connection with a 20-mile four inch gas line between Lloydminster and a dry well hole. If this is indeed the case, I suggest it is time to clean up the bill before us and remove some of the clauses from it.
It is high time these bills were drafted in such a way as to meet the real needs of the company seeking a charter. The legislation before us does not tell us where the operation will start or where it will end. It does not say what the line will carry or what it is intended it shall carry. It says the line may go across interprovincial boundaries. The bill does not say where. It says the line may go across an international boundary, and the nearest international boundary is a long way from the area in which I suppose this line is to be located. The line may carry gas or it may carry oil. All these eventualities are met by the terms of the bill before us.
Many hon. members are interested in a proposition which is still before the house
December 14, 1967

in connection with solids pipe lines. Every one will agree, I think, that solids pipe lines constitute a totally new form of communication which is likely to play a major role in years to come in our economy. Yet this company which proposes to build a 20-mile pipe line has asked for the right to carry solids as well.
Nobody seems to object, though in my opinion the company has very little chance of operating a solids pipe line with the amount of capitalization which is suggested here. I believe it is up to parliament to decide whether companies should be granted these valuable rights. In this case, if the company is a bona fide company, as we are led to believe, I think it should at least remove some of the garbage which is contained in the bill presented to us. I note that the sponsor did not rise here today to tell us he has been in touch with representatives of the company and that they are prepared to have removed from the bill some of the powers they obviously are not likely to use.
What does this company intend to do with a railroad? I am sure the sponsor of the bill will tell us that to his knowledge it does not intend to build one. I believe he would also tell us that to the best of his knowledge it does not intend to build a townsite, or go into the housing business, or buy and lease land, or do all the other things we are being asked to sanction.
If all our legislation were cluttered up with the junk which could be accumulated from other departments not directly concerned we would soon build up the greatest bureaucracy that ever existed. This is not how we handle legislation, and I suggest we follow the same principle in connection with legislation proposed by a private company. I lack sufficient knowledge of the law to explain why the lawyers thought fit to put all this stuff in the bill we are now considering. It certainly sounds stupid. We may get around to reading it all yet. Anyone who looks at it carefully would agree it is stupid, bearing in mind that the avowed purpose of the company concerned is to build a gas line four inches in diameter for a distance of 20 miles.
Some of the powers being requested seem altogether unreasonable. Suppose, for example, this company were to decide to enter upon housing development at the edge of Lloydminster. Despite its limited facilities it would no doubt be able to buy land, raise money, subdivide the land into building lots, establish streets with the necessary sewerage
Private Bills
and drainage, electric light, telephone communications and all the other facilities needed to operate a townsite. I do not know what the people in Alberta would do. I am not sure what the people in Lloydminster would do, but I would be very surprised if they were pleased with the federal government granting this company the right to do these things, and I presume these powers cover expropriation and other necessary measures in the establishment of a townsite. I doubt very much that the municipal and provincial governments will agree with this proposition.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
It is interesting to look at the names of the directors as given in the bill. They include a petroleum executive, a second petroleum executive, a third petroleum executive, a chartered accountant and a solicitor. I suggest that each of these will not be going into the housing development business. I suggest it is probable they will not set up a telecommunications agency or undertake many of the other things mentioned in the bill.
I ask the sponsor of the bill, why does the company want all these powers? In his evidence to the committee the solicitor for the company said that his clients might want to expand. Their pipe line might run across an international boundary but I understand such a boundary is 300 miles away. The company has no reason to build such a pipe line now, but it might. Certainly everything is possible, Mr. Chairman, but usually it is not very likely. I suggest that the likelihood of these people using the powers granted to them in this bill is in the realm of possibility but not likely in the realm of feasibility, advisability or probability.
I think a matter such as this should be of great concern to all hon. members. Such concern on the part of all members is not usually shown just because one person says it should be shown.
