['I say to the hon. member that I am just coming to that in the course of my speech. I might say that I think there has been considerable misunderstanding of what is involved in the marriage breakdown proposal. That proposal was adequately and fully set out in the report of a group that was appointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury in January, 1964. That group reported in 1966. The committee consisted of leading churchmen, lawyers, judges, sociologists, psychiatrists, and even included a politician. The report is embodied in a book entitled, "Putting Asunder". Its subtitle is an interesting one: "A Divorce Law for Contemporary Society". The report says that the essence of the principle of divorce that is based on marriage breakdown is that the court studies and makes findings on the state of the marriage and not on the conduct of the parties. This change of approach is not accomplished by listing a series of circumstances, and saying that they are to constitute a breakdown.
In discussing their conclusion, the writers of the report say this:
We very soon decided that it would not be an improvement, but the reverse, to introduce the principle of breakdown of marriage into the existing law in the shape of additional ground for divorce: and our objections to any such compromise multiplied and hardened as the time went on.
I and others on our committee went through precisely the same mental process. I suspect that others who subject themselves to studying the evidence and thinking about it will emerge with the same conclusions that the English committee emerged with.
In dealing with the choice of alternatives the English committee emerged with.
Although some of our witnesses still had faith in the matrimonial-offence system, our study of it elicited little to its credit and nothing at all to make us want its perpetuation.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the English report was based on a period of 30 years experience with expanded matrimonial offences such as are contemplated in the bill that is presently before the house.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I want to read the conclusion of the committee report on this matter.
Indeed we were persuaded that a divorce law founded on the doctrine of breakdown would not
Divorce Law Reform
only accord better with social realities than the present law does, but would have the merit of showing up divorce for what in essence it is-not a reward for marital virtue on the one side and a penalty for marital delinquency on the other; not a victory for one spouse and a reverse for the other, but a defeat for both, a failure of the marital two-in-oneship in which both its members, however unequal their responsibility, are inevitably involved together. So we arrived at our primary and fundamental recommendation: that the doctrine of the breakdown of marriage should be comprehensively substituted for the doctrine of the matrimonial offence as the basis of all divorce.
The report proceeded to deal fully with what has been the main objection to basing divorce on breakdown, namely that it is not a triable issue and would impose an undue burden on the courts. This is the point of view put forward by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), and I propose to deal with his remarks in more detail later.
May I first call the attention of the house to what the English committee said on this issue?
For the most part we were advised that a judge would not find it unduly difficult to decide, after hearing the evidence, whether or not there was a reasonable probability in all the circumstances of cohabitation being revived. Actions and conduct which under the present law constitute matrimonial offences, though no longer in themselves and by themselves grounds for a decree, would still be available as evidence for breakdown.
It is true, as the minister said-and he gave it as his main reason for turning down this proposal-that this would involve procedural changes. The minister said these changes were unrealistic, and would impose on the existing courts of law and on the judiciary an inquisitorial approach coupled with a broad administrative discretion.
In this statement, the minister differs from the view of the experienced members of the English committee. I suggest he is also overlooking the fact that in this field of family relationships the courts have had to deal with general issues for many years, and deal with them on an administrative basis. For many years the law in Canada has laid down that the custody of children is to be determined on the basis of regard for their welfare. This administrative jurisdiction has existed in English law for centuries since the courts of Chancery exercised a quasi parental jurisdiction over the affairs of children based upon the theory that the crown, which they represented was parens patriae. It is also true that the marriage breakdown theory as applied to divorce would require the', "December 14, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
courts to determine whether the marriage was dead, whether there was any chance of its revival, or whether as it was a mere legal shell. It is not beyond the ability of the courts to do this, and anyone who says it is cannot be too familiar with what the courts are doing now.
It is true that the procedures required in arriving at such decisions would involve a somewhat different approach. This is one of the reasons I am advocating the change. It might involve the assistance of reports from social workers or other experienced people in the community. But there is nothing new in this. In divorce cases in the province of Ontario the rules of the court provide for the receiving of reports from the official guardian which, in turn, he obtains from the children's aid societies, in relation to conditions affecting children of the marriage. I am not sure whether this is the practice in other provinces, but these reports affecting the children are used by the courts to determine the highly important question of the custody of children in divorce cases.
It is said there is a lack of trained and experienced personnel. We have not heard about that from the Canadian Mental Health Association. If there is a lack, then I suggest the existence of a new approach to divorce would undoubtedly direct attention to it and the gap would be filled; more and more people would be trained in this field.
The responsibility would still belong to the court. But to turn down the proposal on the ground that it would introduce a new procedure is to turn it down on an unsatisfactory ground. In conclusion, I wish to refer for a moment to a further passage in the English report which says, in connection with whether the issue of breakdown is triable:
The evidence we have received suggests that Judges would be reluctant to be put in the position of having to make predictions about the future of marriages, but in fact a judgment of breakdown does not require any greater measure of prediction than, for instance, the judgment that the proved conduct of a spouse would, if continued, cause injury to the health of the other spouse. In both cases it is a present probability chat has to be assessed.
The report goes on to give other reasons why one should not mix the breakdown principle with the principle of matrimonial offences. I wish to deal with this subject once again when I return to the question of provision for reconciliation.
In the opinion of the writers of this report who, as I say, were highly experienced, the principle of breakdown ought on no account to be introduced into the existing law in the form of an additional ground. If I may put this in my own words, the tendency of lawyers handling divorce cases would undoubtedly be to avoid basing their cases on breakdown except where they do not fit into any of the other categories. As a result, the basis of the present law would remain; the unreality of determining misconduct would remain. The accusatorial procedure, with all the bitterness it engenders, would remain.
I see it is almost ten o'clock. In the light of these observations I wish to proceed, when I have the opportunity tomorrow, to deal with the general provisions of this bill and to show that unfortunately it does not provide the best solution for the problem of divorce procedure."]

seen or heard of the minister's budget speech interpreted his speech as meaning that he had ditched, jettisoned or rejected the Carter report. And, Mr. Chairman, all of these reports could not be wrong. In any event I will be referring to the minister's words.

The minister and the government clearly have put the report in the waste basket, except perhaps to the extent of including some of the suggestions in the report in the government white paper. Indeed, what the minister said in his speech this afternoon proves that. His attempt now to ditch the report and to hang on to it at the same time in order to have the support of those he is trying to confuse, as well as the support of those who see through the manoeuvre, is just not going to work.

-they will be more in the nature of reforms of the existing tax structure rather than the adoption of a radically different approach.

different approach to our system ol taxation. It does not necessarily mean the adoption of every point made and every recommendation contained in the report. Nobody who gives advice expects that sort of thing to result. But a radically different approach would mean the acceptance of a basic and fundamental change in the taxation system of Canada.
When the minister says that all he is going to do is to reform the existing tax structure and not adopt a radically different approach, he is rejecting the Carter report, and no amount of shaking of the head on the part of the minister will change that fact. He will not be able to fool anybody that he intends to do anything else. I was always impressed, Mr. Chairman, by something I read many years ago written by a writer in Europe on philosophic subjects, who indicated in one of his books-I could not recall during the recess the title of the book-that the most common weakness of all people is a refusal to consider big ideas because of little objections and little difficulties.
I would suggest that when the minister tries to raise questions about the specific details that may or may not be included in the comprehensive tax base recommended by the Carter commission, he too is guilty of this failing. He is trying to divert the attention of the people of Canada from the importance and validity of the report by raising little objections, and is trying to prevent them from recognizing the really great ideas in the report by introducing little prejudices in one direction or another.
I would suggest-and I do not say this offensively-that this is a shabby way to deal with a monumental report, as the minister described it. It is a report which took four and a half years to compile and cost many millions of dollars to produce, using in the process some of the best taxation brains in the country.
As a matter of fact. Mr. Chairman, the commissioners themselves foresaw this situation. I went back to the report to refresh my memory about something that was said on this matter, and I should like to quote a fairly lengthy passage from page two of the first volume, where they say this:
We are fully aware that these conclusions constitute a severe criticism of the present tax system. They were not arrived at lightly nor are they the inevitable result of preconceived opinions. Our bias when we began our task was that the present system was basically sound and compared favourably with the systems of other countries. While we are still of the opinion that the present

Canadian tax system is as good as most other systems, we are convinced that it falls far short of the attainable objectives. We therefore recommend many fundamental changes which, if adopted, would produce a complete transformation and, we believe, result in greater equity and efficiency.
We hope Canadians will accept the challenge implicit in our recommendations. And there can be no doubt that our recommendations constitute a great challenge. Preconceived opinions about taxation are deeply and firmly held. Many will find it extremely difficult to take a new look at old questions. Because some facts cannot be readily ascertained, honest differences of opinion are inevitable.
Then this is the sentence I want to draw to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman:
There is a danger that the debate about these minor factual questions will divert attention from the major issues.
This, Mr. Chairman, is exactly what the minister has tried to do with the Carter report. He has tried to focus attention on minor factual questions and thereby attempt to divert attention from the major issues with which the report deals. I therefore feel confident to repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the statement that the minister has jettisoned the Carter report is a correct and accurate statement, and the minister cannot get out of that situation. Whether or not the reforms of the minister will be adequate from another point of view and whether or not they will be acceptable remains, of course, to be seen when he brings them before parliament.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The minister denied that his budget was intended to increase unemployment. He did not answer this charge directly, and in order not to answer it directly he did what I suppose we all do, Mr. Chairman: He diverted our attention to the United Kingdom. He was ignoring the point by drawing the attention of the members of my party, who proudly have associations with members of the Labour government in Britain, to the fact that that government has pursued policies intended to deflate the economy, with the result of very massive additions to their unemployment rate.
I have only three things to say about that, Mr. Chairman. First, we are not bound, as a party, and we do not intend ever to be bound, by the policies of any other party anywhere else, whether in Canada or elsewhere. I have very grave doubts myself as to whether, if I were in Britain, I would be in entire agreement with the policies there pursued. What is much more important, and
December 14, 1967

what I suggest to the members of the committee questions the relevance if not the honesty of the comparison, is that the minister knows quite well that to compare the problems facing the United Kingdom to the problems facing Canada is to do something that on any basis is not permissible.
They are faced in that country with problems of industrial development, modernization, monetary problems and the fact that sterling is a reserve currency, with all that flows from that. They are different from Canadian problems not merely in degree but in kind. To try to compare what is happening there with what is happening here is surely intellectually a thoroughly impermissible thing to do. Surely, Mr. Chairman, the minister cannot change the effect of his budget by merely pointing to the fact that it was done over there. I remember that the late Mr. G. D. H. Cole, from whom I had the good fortune to learn some things about economics when I attended a university in England some years ago, wrote a little play dealing with the general strike of 1926 in that country. One of the characters in the play was accused by the prime minister of Great Britain of having fomented trouble, a march on 10 Downing street. This character who was thus accused said, "Who, me? No, it's him that did it." Well the minister cannot do that. He cannot say, "Who, me? I did not do anything about unemployment, but Harold Wilson or James Callaghan or whoever it is in Great Britain did."
He is not going to persuade anybody with any intelligence he is dealing with the problem at all when he makes that kind of diverting statement. The fact is the increase in income tax is intended to reduce aggregate demand. The fact is that this increase in income tax, when coupled with other tax increases and coupled, as he and the Minister of National Revenue claim, with massive retrenchment, particularly in the field of construction with its multiplier effect, will necessarily result in increased unemployment. Since I give the minister credit for sufficient intelligence to know that result will follow, I must assume he intended that result. The result will not be accidental.
He and his advisers know greater unemployment will inevitably follow the policies announced in his budget. Since they know unemployment will follow these policies, then they must be assumed to deliberately intend increasing the rate of unemployment in Canada. Again I say you have to study the minister's statement carefully, as I did. When
Ways and Means
he said, "Read my words about the Carter report", he was very careful not to say that he accepted the report. He criticized those of us who said he had ditched it, but at no point in his answer did he say "I accept it" or "I accept the principles of it" or "I accept some of the principles in it". He was very careful not to commit himself.
When he dealt with the charge that he was going deliberately to create increased unemployment, he pointed to the British government. Nowhere in the statement which he made, even this afternoon, did he deny that the result of budget policies will be increased unemployment. In my opinion, the result will inevitably be increased unemployment. He was very careful not to say it. He was very careful not to say to this committee or to the country that in his opinion his budget will not increase unemployment in Canada. I challenge him to rise to his feet now and say just that. If he denies the charge which we make after studying his budget, that the results of these policies will be increased unemployment, then he ought to have the courage to get to his feet and say, "In my opinion unemployment will not increase in this country as a result of these policies". He was very careful not to state that. What he did say in his main speech on November 30, as reported on page 4905 of Hansard-and in more than one place, but the quotation of one short phrase will be enough to make the point:
The fiscal restraints that are essential now may limit somewhat the increase in our production next year but such a limitation now is far better than a serious recession later.
What in heaven's name do the words, "may limit somewhat the increase in our production next year", mean if they do not mean that he knows the results of the budget policies will be a decrease in the rate of growth in this country, and a decreasing rate of growth will necessarily mean increasing unemployment in this country? What does that carefully chosen gobbledegook which I have just quoted from page 4905 of Hansard mean if it does not mean increased unemployment? The minister says that will be the result of his budgetary policy.
As I have said two or three times, there has been a rather puerile attempt to divert us from discussing this serious result of his budget in Canada by trying to twit members of my party with the fact the British government is pursuing a certain policy. This will not hide the fact the minister is pursuing a deliberate policy of unemployment. I will be

December 14, 1967
Ways and Means
happy to be proven wrong if this does not happen, as will every other member in the opposition who shares this view. If I remember correctly, the Leader of the Opposition reached the same conclusion on this point in the budget speech, and I am sure the Leader of the Opposition would be as happy as I and my colleagues would be if we were proven wrong and the minister were proven right.
No one looks forward to even a small increase in unemployment at any time with anything but horror in a country like Canada. I am forced to come to the conclusion, however, after careful study of the minister's policies, that increased unemployment is the inevitable result of these budgetary policies. When that increase in unemployment occurs in the next months the people of Canada will know, and I hope they will for a long time remember, that the gentlemen on the treasury benches deliberately induced that increased unemployment to deal with a situation which might have been dealt with in many other ways.
I know, as I have said, the minister has rejected the Carter report. However, since he said that he will be influenced by it I commend to him the following sentence on page 28 of volume 2 of the report where the commission deals with the kind of inflationary situation we have:
Certainly what is needed is a policy that strikes at those responsible for the inflation rather than a policy that represses aggregate demand and eliminates the inflation only by generating unemployment and general idle capacity.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
This is what the budget is intended to do, generate unemployment and idle capacity, in the hope that that will eliminate the inflation that this country is faced with. The budget, instead, should deal with the forces that are responsible for the present inflationary pressures. I therefore say on behalf of my colleagues, and on my own behalf, that nothing the minister has said can possibly evade the facts, and they are facts, which say that this resolution with respect to income tax is unfair. The burden will fall on the ordinary people of Canada. The tax is not necessary since it does not raise any additional revenue worth anything at all in terms of the total budget. It is deliberately intended to produce unemployment, and in that respect it is antisocial and inhuman.
This totally unfair and unnecessary budget is one of the crosses that the Minister of
fMr. Lewis.]
Finance, who impresses one with his competence and intelligence, will have to carry in an attempt to achieve certain heights which have now apparently become achievable.
Oh, oh.

Before this resolution carries I wish to enter a word of protest on behalf of the married women of this country. I am concerned about the way that the income tax increase affects an especially large group in this country, the women of this country who must work outside their homes.
On previous occasions I have asked whether it would be possible to enact provisions which would allow our working women to deduct from their taxable income expenses which are incurred in connection with the care of their children. While our women are at work someone must look after their children. Since businessmen are allowed deductions with respect to business expenses, could not our working mothers be allowed deductions with respect to the expenses they incur for the care of the children. In the 5 per cent income tax surcharge a special provision is made for our well to do people. The greatest amount that our well to do persons will be asked to pay in addition to their normal income tax is $600.
I urge the minister to give special consideration to the needs of our working women.
I wish that the minister would give me the courtesy of paying attention, because I am speaking for a large group of women in this country.

The minister makes no
comment.

The
Ontario department of labour the other day published a survey which shows that one out of every three workers in Ontario, is a female. In 1941, on the other hand, only one married woman in 20 worked. Today, one married woman out of every four holds down a job outside her home, and a great percentage of these women are in the province of Ontario.
This dramatic rise in the number of women who are employed outside the home can be attributed to the fact that more mothers these days are leaving the home for the office. The more educated a woman is, the greater is the probability that she will work full time after she is married. I wish the
December 14, 1967

minister would listen. In fact, I shall pause in my remarks until I have his attention.
Please.

Half the working wives in the province of Ontario have children who are under 15 years of age. That represents 40 per cent of the women who work outside their homes. If half the working wives in Ontario have children who are under 15 years old, it is high time that consideration be given to allowing child care expenses to be deducted from taxable income in computing income tax. Surely, if businessmen are allowed expense accounts and deductions with respect to business expenses, there is merit in allowing the working wives in this country to deduct from their taxable income the expenses they incur in connection with child care. That makes more sense than increasing the income tax burden for those women who already have a difficult enough time in making arrangements day after day for the care of their families.
Many people brush working wives off with the remark, "These women are just out to get a bit of pin money." Nevertheless, many married women in this country are working and the time for income tax reforms is long overdue. I submit that the minister should give consideration to allowing our working wives a tax rebate. They badly need the money that would be rebated from their income tax to pay for the care of their children.

Ways and Means

I should like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the disastrous effects of the Carter commission report on the mining industry, particularly in British Columbia, will the minister be making an announcement soon regarding the government's intentions in respect of that aspect of the commission report relating to taxation of mining companies?

Nor have I.

speechtext: I have raised this question because I believe that this kind of lip service to Carter, while holding reservations on essential points in the Carter commission report, is not the sort of attitude that my hon. friend would wish his party to adopt.

speechtext: As you well know, Mr. Chairman, we were discussing the income tax resolution when some general speeches were made by members of the New Democratic party, and I felt it was incumbent on me to reply to some of their general contentions. and I say this in a sense of fun rather than by way of criticism-the general discussion on the Carter report was begun by the hon. member's colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West.
The Minister of Finance asked a question a moment ago and I should like to deal with it briefly. For the record, whether the hon. gentleman is interested or not, our party, last July held a federal convention-

Just a moment. Wait.
Stick to the rules.

At that time we adopted a policy of support for the Carter report. It is in line with this policy that I and others in this party have made our comments.
In the second place, we do agree with the idea of a comprehensive tax base. Mr. Chairman, I have not had the opportunity to speak on this resolution yet, but I now wish to protest against the tax increase that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is asking us to approve today. I object to that increase for several reasons.
The first is that when taxes are increased, usually something is given in return. The resolutions under consideration are designed to increase taxes and do not provide anything in return. On the contrary, works are cancelled, reductions are made, a check of the economic development is sought and, at the same time, taxes are increased. I find this completely unacceptable. If, at least, the people were given something for the additional money extracted from them by force. What they get is a cut in expenditures, fewer work projects, but all the same taxes are being levied. Why? If we are to increase taxes, we should give our people something in return. But this is not what is being done. We raise taxes, but we give nothing; on the contrary, we take something away. So, that is the first reason why I object to this resolution.
The second reason, Mr. Chairman, is that I feel we should be sick and tired of having two governments, one in Ottawa and one in Quebec, one after the other, each in turn, raising our taxes. We are the only nation in the world to be separately taxed by two governments, both of which levy income taxes.
The jurisdictions are really spread around and the same goes for us here.
I admit that Ontario does not have a minister of revenue and that the federal government collects taxes from the citizens in that province and then transfers them to the provincial government. But in Quebec we have two: one provincial minister of revenue and another minister of revenue in Ottawa. That means that we have two ministers of revenue to increase taxes alternately. Of course, we always have increases. When taxes do not go up in Ontario, they go up in Quebec; when not in Quebec, then in Ottawa. That is the system we know. I see some Liberal members from Quebec seem to like that. "Come on with the taxes". They were not called "taxers" for nothing. We had "Jean la taxe" in Quebec; we now have "Sharp the Taxer" in Ottawa, and the Liberal members from Quebec accept that.
Ways and Means
I wonder how the Minister of Finance can start his campaign for the leadership of the Liberal party under such bad auspices. In fact, he is starting on the wrong foot, with taxes.
It is none of your business.

Can you see that, Mr. Chairman? He is only the minister of taxes. How would he be if he were Prime Minister?
So, Mr. Chairman, I want to protest against these taxes and I even want to move an amendment to the resolution. So I shall ask my good friend, the member for Rober-val (Mr. Gauthier) to second the amendment.

Clause (1) provides that for the year 1968 and subsequent taxation years, income tax shall be increased by 5 per cent. It is called a special surtax. There are all kinds of designations. Sometimes, it is taxes; other times, it is surtaxes, to show the people they are overtaxed.
That is why it is called thus: it adds up to a lot.

Let the government ask anything it wants from the companies, but the people, I think, already pay enough taxes. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I will resume my remarks where they were interrupted on December 5 last.
I was putting forward my second argument in support of the indissolubility of marriage through the very nature of love.
First of all, this supposes a love-match and not a marriage of convenience or interest. A notable proportion of the petitions for divorce stem from this marriage of convenience which we cannot advise against too much. Experience has proved that marriage without love does not last long. The parties involved very soon turn to divorce.
If it is a marriage for love, the nature of such love remains to be known. A marriage based on physical attraction only, on sex-appeal only, purely on sexual instinct finding satisfaction in the physical charms of the spouse, such marriage is as precarious and shaky as physical love itself. Love based only on physical attractiveness and in which sexual instinct finds satisfaction cannot last. In no time at all, it will crumble. This is a cause of another goodly proportion of petitions for divorce. They are marriages mostly gone into by couples while still minors. One could never advise often enough against these early marriages without sufficient proof of true love.
However, those marriages are quite valid, even if they are based on physical and psychological love, without any depth. The indissolubility of such marriages, which are not deeply rooted by this precarious love, finds its basis in the explicit will of the contracting parties, expressed in all freedom and lucidity. I will come back to that point later on.
A marriage contracted in an atmosphere of genuine love which supersedes, yet includes, purely physical love, essentially admits of an absolute and irrevocable bond of faithfulness. Let all those who married under the influ-uence of genuine love call upon their own experience; they will soon feel that the indissolubility of marriage is intimately bound with the constancy of love. Provisional love,

December 14, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
short-term faithfulness, those are contradictory terms. The daily experience of true lovers demonstrates this. How often they promise to be true to each other in life and death! How often they plight their troth! If one of them were to say: "I will love you for two years", the other could rightly answer: "In that case, you do not really love me." The basic reason of all this is that true love is necessarily faithful and irrevocable. At the beginning of all true love there is the intention of being absolutely, definitively and permanently faithful. The lover will not love where he does not intend to be faithful. How real, then, should be conjugal fidelity which is based on the most intimate relationship that can exist between two people, a relationship sealed in the physical union of two bodies! I could elaborate on this point, but I think this will suffice to show the strong basis on which rests the indissolubility of marriage. However, I will add two con-firmatur.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
First, the exclusive character of true love indicates the necessity for an absolute and irrevocable fidelity. It is a fact ascertained daily that two lovers do not admit a third party between them. What is the origin of jealousy in love if not from the fact that true love excludes any person other than the parties concerned. As soon as one of the two goes towards a third party, the other suffers, and how! Love tragedies, suicides resulting from deluded and unrequited love find an explanation in that. These facts illustrate in a concrete way the necessity for an absolute and irrevocable fidelity in love.
Secondly, if we take a look at forms used to certify the existence of marriage, whether in the civil tribunal or the religious tribunal, we always find this little formula: until death do you part. Why that? On what is this little formula based?
What does it express exactly, if not a requirement for absolute and irrevocable fidelity? And to bless the remarriage of divorced people with those words: until death do you part, seems to me a monumental farce which alters to a considerable extent the seriousness of fidelity and love.
Thirdly, the indissolubility of marriage is based on a contractual promise. Marriage is looked upon as a contract. Therefore, it comes under the law. A special obligation of fidelity results from a promise given and accepted by words, signs or equivalent acts.

Two beings are tied to one another by contract and that until death do them part. Some might say that any contract can be terminated if both parties to it so desire. That is true and that is the reason why I do not insist too much on the indissolubility of marriage. However, I wish to point out that the object of the marriage contract is not outside things. The interested parties are the main object of it, which makes the marriage contract a unique contract. Individuals have an absolute value and nobody can dispose of them at will as can be done for purely material objects. I therefore believe that the indissolubility of marriage is also based on a special obligation of fidelity which does not only proceed from love as such, but from a given and accepted promise.
In concluding this first part, Mr. Speaker, owing to the divine will concerning the nature of true love and a mutual and contractual promise, it must be admitted that indissolubility is an essential characteristic of marriage. It is therefore ascribable to natural law. Since such is the case, there follows an inevitable consequence, to wit that no human institution a fortiori, nor any individual can break marriage ties without going beyond his rights. This statement does not prejudge the quite exceptional cases which can occur beyond the scope of those principles. But a worthwhile reflection must be based on duly recognized principles rather than on exceptional cases. My views on divorce can be readily appreciated. But before dealing more specifically with this matter, let us draw a last corollary from the preceding remarks.
Our modern world rejects indissolubility as an extreme requirement for a normal marriage. Among other fatal remedies, it proposes what is commonly called trial marriage. Of course, such a sexual union, deprived of the intentional faithfulness and responsibility of genuine love, has nothing to do with a true marriage. To try marriage is about as sensible as trying death in an extended sleep. Trial marriage to me is the same as public concubinage.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to consider the attitude of the state toward divorce.
As we have seen in the first part of these thoughts, indissolubility of marriage to which divorce is opposed arises directly from natural law as such. Now, the principles of natural law are absolute standards. Thus, there is not and cannot be a true dispensation from a natural, moral law. As a result, divorce, which purports to be a dispensation from the natural law of marriage, a dispensation of
December 14, 1967

indissolubility, is totally objectionable because it undermines the very basis of marriage which God decreed to be indissoluble. Does that mean that the state should adopt toward divorce an attitude of total prohibition? No, as we shall see later on. The impossibility of a true dispensation does not preclude the possibility of a legal tolerance. It will be the first point of the following thoughts. Then, we shall briefly consider the motives likely to legitimize such a tolerance. Finally, we shall put forward some remedies likely to control a social ill which is contaminating an entire nation.
First, the possibility of the legal tolerance of divorce. Let us first recall some guiding principles.
The Church alone can legislate on marriage between Christians, that is baptized people. The state alone has the right to legislate on the marriage of non-Christians, that is to say non-baptized people but, of course, only in the framework of the natural institution. As far as marriage of Christians is concerned, the state has exclusive rights on the civil effects of the marriage (for instance, right of succession, legal guardianship, family allowances, etc.).
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
When mention is made of religious divorce or civil divorce, strictly speaking and in principle, it can only involve the breakdown of the matrimonial bond. Even after the religious or civil judgment, except certain most exceptional cases, the matrimonial bond is always there because it is permanent by nature. Such a judgment can only ensure certain religious or certain legal or civil effects.
In the light of these principles, let us clarify the attitude of the state while I shall summarize in this way:
Always, the morality of right had to face the question of whether a legal tolerance and the regulating of bad things are allowed and may be more prudent than total interdiction which, through the wickedness of man, may have worse consequences. For instance, since St. Augustine, numerous theologians have held as licit the legal regulation and, therefore, the tolerance of controlled prostitution, provided this did not result in the apparent moral justification of vice and the multiplication of offences. Similarly, Christian politicians and jurists can participate in the legal regulation of civil divorce, but only if the legislation does not multiply the divorce 27053-344i
Divorce Law Reform
offences and does not give the impression that those same Christian politicians and jurists approve morally what they believe they cannot prevent legally. The tolerance or, rather, the legal damming up of an evil reality must, as a whole, serve morality.
I, therefore, define my opinion in five points.
(1)	Divorce is, and will always be, a moral offence, because it is contrary to an essential and natural propriety of marriage. This must be clearly evident in the civil legislation or, better still, the civil legislation must not be such that it presents divorce as something which is normally beyond reproach.
(2)	As already stated, none but God should have the power to allow a true exemption from this natural law called indissolubility of marriage. However, a duly established institution such as the state may accept a legal tolerance and legislate accordingly.
(3)	In conclusion I say once more, because this seems to be of crucial importance, that civil legislation should not be established under any colour of moral legalization of divorce. Tolerance does not mean moral approval. On the contrary, the whole civil legislation system of the state, more precisely its marriage legislation, must be geared above all towards family happiness, the preservation of chastity and the durability of natural marriage.
Modern society, which seeks any number of grounds for divorce and increases the frailty of marital unions through legislation on the property of married couples and other arbitrary provisions of marriage laws, digs its own grave.
(4)	If society can tolerate divorce, while trying to decrease its frequency, it can also tolerate marriage between divorcees to ensure its civil effects only.
(5)	In practice, society will have to consider each individual case with the utmost care. It will have to carefully consider the alleged motives of the litigants and, especially, ensure maximum security for the children. We have no right to allow innocent children to feel the effects of the marriage breakdown.
These few considerations, however schematic, are enough to allow the legislators to undertake a sound discussion. Now, let us look into the grounds which can justify this tolerance on the part of the state with regard to divorce.
There can be many grounds, all more or less valid. However, my attention is caught more particularly by four of them.

December 14, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
The first one is the non-consummation of a valid marriage. Marriage is consummated after sexual relations. If a sexual act has not taken place, the marriage can be annulled. Since there has not been real sexual union, we cannot really speak of an indissoluble marital tie. This situation can happen quite often when the two spouses, for some reason or other, had no opportunity of living together after the marriage took place. If they have lived together, the marriage is presumed to have been consummated.
Secondly, the impossibility of a peaceful cohabitation where one of the spouses, most often, the wife, is victim of the brutality of the other or of a professed hatred. This ground is more imperative if the children of the marriage must live in an infernal atmosphere. Of two evils, one must choose the lesser.
Thirdly, adultery may be a valid ground. The infidelity of one of the spouses deprives them of every right to a complete partnership between husband and wife. Even if condonation is an ideal, one can understand the unbearable situation of the spouse who remained faithful.
Fourth, the definitive and unjustified desertion of one of the spouses, especially if the children of the marriage suffer by that in a special way.
The grounds could be manifold. But I would like to point out two things about them. All grounds are not to be accepted simultaneously. It is absolutely necessary to limit them; otherwise, we will be opening the door to anarchy in society. The legislators must adopt only a few, those which seem the most imperative, according to the situation in the country.
Any civil legislation that really wants to put a stop to divorce, that social evil, will have to be demanding with regard to the procedure to be followed. That will be a way to emphasize the disapproval aroused by such a state of affairs. It will be most important to find out whether the husband and wife deliberately made up the grounds which could justify their divorce petition. It must be recognized that whoever wants to leave the other can easily and with the explicit intention of getting a divorce create the unfortunate situation which would justify such a petition to the state. The latter must therefore be in a position to bring to light that deceitful intention.
In short, Mr. Speaker, even if civil law recognizes the validity of certain grounds
[Mr. Simard.l
for divorce, this law and the judicial procedure to be followed must be established in such a way that people can say that it is not easy to get a divorce in Canada. If they say the opposite, it is a sign that the state morally approves divorce and accepts the practice on a wide scale. Therefore, such legislation is harmful and fully deserves the censure and indignation of all those who still possess a remnant of natural morality. The state itself,
I repeat, is digging its own grave. The experience of foreign states in past centuries is quite revelatory with regard to this unescapable consequence. If part of the population has lost all natural sense of morality, the lawmakers must show some instead, even though it is sad indeed to realize that such a substitution is necessary.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
And what of the remedial action to be promoted against divorce? The state must therefore take a negative attitude toward divorce, that is, show its disapproval by being exacting with regard to grounds for divorce, as well as to the legal procedure to be followed. But it must not restrict its role to a negative attitude. A squarely positive position is perhaps the best way to check that disease. Such a positive position should consist in promoting, by every means possible, the indissolubility of marriage. Those means are many and varied. I shall point out a few.
Through special grants, the state should promote and encourage social organizations whose main purpose is to protect the family and the marital community. For instance, several institutions are designed to prepare future spouses properly. Others bring together couples with some experience of married and family life, to study some specific problems peculiar to married people and to strengthen finally the bonds which unite them. Other agencies work toward the reconciliation of separated spouses. It seems to me that the government should give positive help to such agencies which contribute to the welfare of society in general, and of the marriage institution in particular.
To prevent under-age weddings, which are too frequent, society should, for instance, further promote youth recreational activities which aim at the development and flowering of young people in a healthy climate. Even if some young people sometimes commit the well-known blunder, society should provide them with some protection against shotgun weddings, as they are called. The parents of
December 14, 1967

those young people have no right, even to hide a certain shame, to push them into a marriage they do not want. One evil cannot be cured by another evil.
Finally, it might perhaps be well to review all our statutes on marriage, and see it they really serve the family well, and do not burden it with certain obligations which, in the final analysis, are detrimental to the strength of marriage. Some spouses consider giving up marriage because the state imposes obligations upon them which they did not have in single life.
Many other ways could be enumerated, Mr. Speaker, but it is up to us, legislators in this house, to seek and find the most efficient means to reinforce the stability, the indissolubility of matrimonial ties and to stem the social evil of divorce. The state should always endeavour to promote variously the solidity of that small cell which the family, the conjugal community constitutes. Is society not made up of thousands of such small cells? If the cells deteriorate and break down under the influence of divorce-cancer, what will happen to the great body, society? Deteriorating cells indicate a dying, or already dead, organism. However, if cells are teeming with life, that is, if the married community maintains an indefectible stability, the organism as a whole will be in a state of growth and sound development, in other words, society is on the straight road to full development.

Mr. Speaker, when this matter was discussed at the resolution stage I welcomed the fact that at long last we had a bill for the reform of our divorce laws which had been introduced by the government. I must admit when I saw the bill itself it was a serious disappointment. It now represents a considerable improvement from the existing law of Canada, but it is not very difficult to accomplish this because the existing law of Canada, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) pointed out, was either pre-confederation law or the law of England of 1857 as modified in 1870. The existing law of Canada is so antiquated and has produced such grave hardships that any change in it was bound to be an improvement. However, the bill goes very little if any further, than the changes made in the law of Great Britain in the 1930's.
I think it is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that when parliament at last tackles the problem
Divorce Law Reform
of divorce it does not take advantage of the British experience. It is too bad that the law, as introduced by this government, is not atuned to contemporary society or to the needs of the second half of the twentieth century. It is to be regretted the government has not seen fit to listen to the advice of the churches, although the government does refer to this advice. When I say "the churches", I mean almost all of the recognized churches in Canada. They have advocated a totally new approach, an approach based upon the concept of marriage breakdown. This is a totally different way of handling the problem of divorce from the old concept of matrimonial offences. The basic philosophy behind this new approach, known as marriage breakdown, was enunciated, so far as I know, by Lord Walker, one of the members of a royal commission on marriage in 1955, who said:
The true significance of marriage, as I see it, is lifelong cohabitation in the home for the family. But when the prospect of continuing cohabitation has ceased, that true view of the significance of marriage seems to require that the legal ties should be dissolved. Each empty tie-as empty ties accumulate-adds increasing harm to the community and injury to the ideal of marriage.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the bill before us makes a sort of verbal nod to the breakdown theory but, as I shall point out, it rejects that theory in essence. The matter was very well put by one of the English law lords in a debate in the House of Lords in June, 1963 when he said this:
There are only two theories alive in this problem -namely, are we going to act on the matrimonial offence or are we going to act on the breakdown of marriage theory? That is the fight.
That is still the fight here.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The bill which the minister has introduced mixes up the two theories of matrimonial offence and marriage breakdown, and the melange is neither logical nor sound. It contains other defects which I shall try to point out and rectify by way of amendments when we reach the committee stage. I know that the minister has promised to take seriously such amendments as may be presented in committee.
Once again this government has put the members of the House of Commons on the horns of a dilemma. It has introduced a bill which contains serious defects, both in its basic approach to the matter with which it deals and in its details. Nevertheless it may be impossible for us to reject this bill as its

December 14, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
provisions contain a great advance, as I have already said, over the existing law. It is just too bad that once again we are asked to accept the second best.
Before I discuss some of the major faults of the bill may I say that certain features of it should be welcomed. The first of those is the provision with respect to Canadian domicile, whereby the domicile of a married woman shall be determined as if she were unmarried. That means in effect that a married woman can bring her action for divorce where she lives. This reform is long overdue. The old rule that a husband's domicile prevailed was based on an English judicial decision, which in turn was based on the survival of the theory of the unity of the spouses. The theory in effect was that the wife had no separate existence apart from that of her husband. I think that any married man in this house will say that that theory was not founded on fact.

speechtext:
The theory, apart from its hoary nature, has worked grave hardships. I am glad that that matter is being changed.
I also welcome the final elimination of parliamentary divorce and the conferring on the Exchequer Court of Canada of jurisdiction to pronounce divorces, pending the acceptance of jurisdiction by the Superior Court of Quebec and the Supreme Court of Newfoundland. It is not necessary to recall the long battle that was waged by my colleagues, the hon. members for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and Skeena (Mr. Howard) to bring about this reform and to remove from parliament the responsibility of exercising a judicial responsibility which it was in no way fitted to discharge.
We welcome, further, the fact that the bill grants to the courts the right to deal with corollary relief, that is to say, those questions to do with the maintenance and custody of the children of the marriage and the payment of alimony to deserving spouses. It is my view that any law would be irresponsible if it failed to provide that the authority which dissolved the marriage could, at the same time, have authority to deal with the obligations that have arisen out of and been created by the marriage.

I welcome another feature of the bill which recognizes the duty of the courts to be concerned with the question of reconciliation. For reasons which I shall go into later, I have come to the conclusion that the provisions in the present bill, divorced as they are from the new approach of marriage breakdown, may turn out to be of little effect. It is however, some comfort that the existence of this problem is recognized.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, so far as the good aspects of the bill are concerned, if the grounds for divorce are to be expanded instead of the new theory of marriage breakdown being adopted, I welcome the extension of these grounds to include physical and mental cruelty, rendering continued cohabitation intolerable. We welcome the recognition that where a marriage has broken down and has resulted in an extended period of separation, that that marriage then should be dissolved.
Having recognized and welcomed these features of the bill, let me now turn to what I consider to be the basic defect. That is, as I have said before, the rejection of marriage breakdown as the sole ground for dissolution of the marriage. As I said before, this approach was put forward to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons by a number of highly responsible groups: the United Church of Canada, the Anglican Church of Canada, the National Council of Women, the Canadian Mental Health Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Canadian Committee on the Status of Women and a number of individuals who are experienced in this field.
I have just this week received a communication from the Family Services Association of metropolitan Toronto which points out that in the second annual report of the British Law Commission of 1967 the following statement is to be found:
We are satisfied that if parliament were to accept the principle of breakdown as the basis of divorce, practical and feasible proposals making use of the separation grounds could be prepared for the consideration of parliament.

speechtext:
I say to the hon. member that I am just coming to that in the course of my speech. I might say that I think there has been considerable misunderstanding of what is involved in the marriage breakdown proposal. That proposal was adequately and fully set out in the report of a group that was appointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury in January, 1964. That group reported in 1966. The committee consisted of leading churchmen, lawyers, judges, sociologists, psychiatrists, and even included a politician. The report is embodied in a book entitled, "Putting Asunder". Its subtitle is an interesting one: "A Divorce Law for Contemporary Society". The report says that the essence of the principle of divorce that is based on marriage breakdown is that the court studies and makes findings on the state of the marriage and not on the conduct of the parties. This change of approach is not accomplished by listing a series of circumstances, and saying that they are to constitute a breakdown.
In discussing their conclusion, the writers of the report say this:
We very soon decided that it would not be an improvement, but the reverse, to introduce the principle of breakdown of marriage into the existing law in the shape of additional ground for divorce: and our objections to any such compromise multiplied and hardened as the time went on.
I and others on our committee went through precisely the same mental process. I suspect that others who subject themselves to studying the evidence and thinking about it will emerge with the same conclusions that the English committee emerged with.
In dealing with the choice of alternatives the English committee emerged with.
Although some of our witnesses still had faith in the matrimonial-offence system, our study of it elicited little to its credit and nothing at all to make us want its perpetuation.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the English report was based on a period of 30 years experience with expanded matrimonial offences such as are contemplated in the bill that is presently before the house.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I want to read the conclusion of the committee report on this matter.
Indeed we were persuaded that a divorce law founded on the doctrine of breakdown would not
Divorce Law Reform
only accord better with social realities than the present law does, but would have the merit of showing up divorce for what in essence it is-not a reward for marital virtue on the one side and a penalty for marital delinquency on the other; not a victory for one spouse and a reverse for the other, but a defeat for both, a failure of the marital two-in-oneship in which both its members, however unequal their responsibility, are inevitably involved together. So we arrived at our primary and fundamental recommendation: that the doctrine of the breakdown of marriage should be comprehensively substituted for the doctrine of the matrimonial offence as the basis of all divorce.
The report proceeded to deal fully with what has been the main objection to basing divorce on breakdown, namely that it is not a triable issue and would impose an undue burden on the courts. This is the point of view put forward by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), and I propose to deal with his remarks in more detail later.
May I first call the attention of the house to what the English committee said on this issue?
For the most part we were advised that a judge would not find it unduly difficult to decide, after hearing the evidence, whether or not there was a reasonable probability in all the circumstances of cohabitation being revived. Actions and conduct which under the present law constitute matrimonial offences, though no longer in themselves and by themselves grounds for a decree, would still be available as evidence for breakdown.
It is true, as the minister said-and he gave it as his main reason for turning down this proposal-that this would involve procedural changes. The minister said these changes were unrealistic, and would impose on the existing courts of law and on the judiciary an inquisitorial approach coupled with a broad administrative discretion.
In this statement, the minister differs from the view of the experienced members of the English committee. I suggest he is also overlooking the fact that in this field of family relationships the courts have had to deal with general issues for many years, and deal with them on an administrative basis. For many years the law in Canada has laid down that the custody of children is to be determined on the basis of regard for their welfare. This administrative jurisdiction has existed in English law for centuries since the courts of Chancery exercised a quasi parental jurisdiction over the affairs of children based upon the theory that the crown, which they represented was parens patriae. It is also true that the marriage breakdown theory as applied to divorce would require the

December 14, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
courts to determine whether the marriage was dead, whether there was any chance of its revival, or whether as it was a mere legal shell. It is not beyond the ability of the courts to do this, and anyone who says it is cannot be too familiar with what the courts are doing now.
It is true that the procedures required in arriving at such decisions would involve a somewhat different approach. This is one of the reasons I am advocating the change. It might involve the assistance of reports from social workers or other experienced people in the community. But there is nothing new in this. In divorce cases in the province of Ontario the rules of the court provide for the receiving of reports from the official guardian which, in turn, he obtains from the children's aid societies, in relation to conditions affecting children of the marriage. I am not sure whether this is the practice in other provinces, but these reports affecting the children are used by the courts to determine the highly important question of the custody of children in divorce cases.
It is said there is a lack of trained and experienced personnel. We have not heard about that from the Canadian Mental Health Association. If there is a lack, then I suggest the existence of a new approach to divorce would undoubtedly direct attention to it and the gap would be filled; more and more people would be trained in this field.
The responsibility would still belong to the court. But to turn down the proposal on the ground that it would introduce a new procedure is to turn it down on an unsatisfactory ground. In conclusion, I wish to refer for a moment to a further passage in the English report which says, in connection with whether the issue of breakdown is triable:
The evidence we have received suggests that Judges would be reluctant to be put in the position of having to make predictions about the future of marriages, but in fact a judgment of breakdown does not require any greater measure of prediction than, for instance, the judgment that the proved conduct of a spouse would, if continued, cause injury to the health of the other spouse. In both cases it is a present probability chat has to be assessed.
The report goes on to give other reasons why one should not mix the breakdown principle with the principle of matrimonial offences. I wish to deal with this subject once again when I return to the question of provision for reconciliation.
In the opinion of the writers of this report who, as I say, were highly experienced, the principle of breakdown ought on no account to be introduced into the existing law in the form of an additional ground. If I may put this in my own words, the tendency of lawyers handling divorce cases would undoubtedly be to avoid basing their cases on breakdown except where they do not fit into any of the other categories. As a result, the basis of the present law would remain; the unreality of determining misconduct would remain. The accusatorial procedure, with all the bitterness it engenders, would remain.
I see it is almost ten o'clock. In the light of these observations I wish to proceed, when I have the opportunity tomorrow, to deal with the general provisions of this bill and to show that unfortunately it does not provide the best solution for the problem of divorce procedure.
I should like to ask the leader of the house whether there is any change in the business for tomorrow and whether he can indicate the business for next week.

COMPANY OF YOUNG CANADIANS-REPORTED SUBSIDIZATION OF PRIVATE SCHOOL IN B.C.
speechtext:
My question arises from an article which appeared in Maclean's magazine for December, 1967, "Maclean's Reports". It is about an unusual school in Vancouver which has grown up in response to the wishes of half a dozen or so disgruntled students from Lord Byng high school who complained about the high school system. By the end of the summer this group had grown to about 20 youngsters aged between 12 and 18 from all over Vancouver. They appealed for help from the Company of Young Canadians and in response, Colin Thomson, a 20-year-old graduate from the University of British

December 14, 1967	COMMONS
Columbia and a C.Y.C. employee, agreed to work as co-ordinator. So they set about developing a rather unusual school.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
They were able to rent space in Vancouver. They were able to obtain a library by lugging their own collections of books from home, which does not sound very much like a poverty stricken clientele and, as this article reports:
Their 1,000 volume collection leans more heavily on John Lennon and Henry Miller than it does on Shakespeare.
The problem of full-time teachers was almost insurmountable until the efforts of Mr. Thomson were augmented when the Company of Young Canadians, as this article reports, "agreed to underwrite salaries for five full-time staff members". But I learned by checking that there are three full-time staff members from the Company of Young Canadians at this unusual school.
I quote further from the article:
To achieve the freedom they want, the kids have thrown out formal lessons, exams, report cards, grades, predetermined curriculum and timetables.
Instead they have something called independent study. They stay home for days, if they are working on a project. They organize field trips, and have heard a Buddhist monk lecture on Viet Nam.
As I read this article it struck me that this was a rather unusual engagement for an organization that was supposed to be one of the main arms to be used in the drive in the war on poverty. I looked up the act establishing the company, and find that in the objects and powers defined in section 15 the company may:
-engage in community development work in urban and rural areas in Canada:
organize and carry out programs designed primarily to widen the social and economic opportunities of young people who leave school before completing their schooling;
organize and carry out programs. .. to reduce the number of young people who leave school before completing their schooling;
assist vocational training projects... undertake recreation programs for young people where recreation programs are not available;
undertake programs in public health-
And so on. All of these deal with poverty as we ordinarily recognize it. When the act was introduced in this house the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself said:
It is important to note, Mr. Speaker, that in all such proposed projects or programs the company would operate only in co-operation with the many 27053-345
DEBATES	5463
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion other organizations and agencies already in the field which are already attempting to deal with these social and economic problems.
I would maintain nothing is in the field of education as much as the public school system of British Columbia, but here we have the Company of Young Canadians going completely outside its mandate, not to cooperate with that school system but in a very real sense to subvert it.
Checking again, I found there was no cooperation either with the provincial department of education or the Vancouver school board. The entire project has been set up without the least co-operation from there, and it is being treated as another private school. Unless there is a complaint from a parent or from a student within the school it will not normally be investigated by the provincial department or by the Vancouver school board.
What I am really interested in are the constitutional points that this experiment raises. Although the volunteers from the Company of Young Canadians may not be receiving any direct grant, or a salary from the school, nevertheless their expenses are paid through the company. Taking these three teachers as a fraction of the 180 volunteers in the field, and allotting them a percentage of the total budget for the company last year, we find that providing these volunteers for this school for middle class and wealthy students, costs the taxpayers of Canada well over $13,000. It does not matter how indirect it is, the subsidy is there. It seems this is a strange intrusion of the federal authority into the field of education.
I would be interested to know if other provinces in the country can expect the same sort of treatment that is being provided to British Columbia. We who come from British Columbia know very well that on a variety of aid programs we have had to battle tooth and nail in order to get federal assistance for that province, and so it seems strange that this organization can move so openly in opposition to the existing organization, indeed in contempt of the existing organization, to set up a school system the virtue of which is highly doubtful, and the operation of which has nothing whatever to do with the sort of poverty that was contemplated when the act setting up the Company of Young Canadians was being debated and passed by this parliament.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO NEXT STEPS
TRANSPORT-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO NEXT STEPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today in the question period I raised with the Prime Minister the matter of further details with reference to his press statement of yesterday, when he indicated to the general public that there would be no scrapping of the Prince Edward Island crossing project. I think Prince Edward Islanders and many other Canadians can be forgiven if they become increasingly sceptical about the future of this project. Indeed I find it difficult to obtain support in any quarter for the belief that the government is in fact serious about the continuance of this project. Some people suggest there never was any seriousness on the part of the government, even in the early stages, in respect of pursuing this project. I find this difficult to believe.
Since I am not privileged to know about the various discussions going on in cabinet circles about this matter, it is difficult for me to know the actual state of mind which exists with regard to this particular project. However, I must admit that if people had some doubt concerning the furtherance of the Prince Edward Island-New Brunswick crossing, they must have had that uncertainty heightened to a considerable degree when only a few short hours following the release of the announcement that the project would continue the man who made that announcement indicated his own resignation.
I do not suggest there is a connection between these two events, but I do suggest, if the government expects to be taken seriously in the matter of dealing with this most important project, that it is high time we had some action. It is an important project, not only to the end that it will achieve for the first time a permanent means of transportation to and
[Mr. Johnston.)

from two provinces of Canada, but also it is important-as will be realized by those concerned about this, if they investigate the matter-from the standpoint of the future standard of living which may be enjoyed by the people of Prince Edward Island.
I would think that this government and indeed any government ought to be concerned about the fact that there are provinces of Canada which have a standard of living much below the standard of living in other parts of Canada. It is a fact well known to members of this house that the standard of living in the Atlantic region is at a figure of roughly 70 per cent of the national average. Until major steps are taken by the national government to rectify the serious problems which face this region we will never effectively achieve a national standard truly enjoyed by people in all parts of the country.
I believe this crossing is fundamentally important because it involves two great problems which confront Prince Edward Island-ders. One of these problems is transportation. If we wish to become competitive in the manufacturing business related to our basic industries of farming and fishing, it is imperative that we have the kind of transportation which can only be provided by a causeway or crossing facility. I think this is well understood by most people.
Of almost equal importance to Prince Edward Island is the whole business of a power link which, as I understand it, will come with the establishment of the crossing. The idea of s submarine power cable has been accepted for some time now. However, Prince Edward Islanders cannot look forward to the benefits to be derived from large amounts of low cost electric power until that crossing is completed. There is the third argument that the national government at the present time is expending annually $5 million in the form of a subsidy to make up the difference in the cost of the present ferry transportation service.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
These are all good economic reasons for all Canadians to be concerned about the future of the Northumberland strait crossing. Yet, during the past two years we have seen the most unusual performance ever witnessed on the part of this government. On several occasions in the house we have been told that the government is not going to do this right now-that at some time they plan to get it
December 14, 1967	COMMONS
under way, or that at the moment it is being reviewed.
It is not my concern and intention this evening to bring out the many questions and comments that have been made in this house because they are all of public record, and known. What concerns me, and the reason I asked the question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon, is the hope that we can get some assurance from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) that in the next few days we can expect some schedule indicating that the people of Prince Edward Island and of Canada generally may be assured that the project is going ahead, rather than some general statement that the government is committed to maintaining a transportation link, which is something I find now a bit devious. I hope to get a firm commitment that a permanent link will be established, whether it involves a complete causeway, or a causeway, tunnel and bridge complex, which will be established and built in the shortest possible time; because this makes good business sense and will provide the kind of economic opportunity this island province both needs and desires.
I find it very difficult to accept, as I am sure that people do, that in the two budgets which have been presented in just a little over a year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) on one occasion and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) on another occasion have taken what I thought was a light approach, that they could with complete abandonment suggest that this project could be deferred, delayed, rescheduled-whatever euphemism you want to use-and expect the people to be satisfied.
Therefore I ask the Minister of Public Works to give the members of this house and the people of Prince Edward Island some assurance that we may have some specific assurance shortly, rather than the usual generality that tells us very little and fills us with great disappointment.

This next item is most important to many of my hon. friends from the maritime provinces. The government has decided to defer the placing of any further new contracts for the Northumberland causeway, pending a thorough review of the situation by Col. Edward Churchill, whose services have been retained as a co-ordinator of the project. This review, made necessary by the drastic escalation in the estimated cost of the project as originally conceived, will include the examination of alternative ways of meeting, on a more economically justifiable basis the commitment of the federal government to the government and the people of Prince Edward Island.
There was an interjection following, which the minister stated:
That commitment this government will keep.

There is no thought of scrapping the P.E.I. crossing project.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Revenue Minister Benson told the House of Commons on December 7 that the federal government would keep its commitment to the people of Prince Edward Island. I now confirm what he said.
We intend to proceed with the project. In fact, we are busy on it now. Colonel Edward Churchill is now actively directing a full review of the plans made by Northumberland Consultants Limited.
We believe that the people of Prince Edward Island want us to honour our commitment in the most efficient and practical way. I have asked Colonel Churchill that there be no delay in completing a thorough review of the plans and this review is proceeding at full pace.
That engineering review is going on extremely well at the moment. I cannot give a definite date as to when it will be completed. I cannot foretell what precise form of crossing will be recommended in the review.
